utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you and good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Today is Tuesday, 26th of February, 2008. Good morning to the Prosecution. Good morning, Witness. Good morning, Mr. Seselj. And good morning to everyone assisting us in this case. We'll now proceed with the cross-examination of the witness. The accused, and I'd like to thank him for this, has given us three large binders. We've all received them at the Bench. I suppose that the Prosecutor have received them as well, and the witness will thus be able to follow the cross-examination more easily. Unless Mr. Seselj has any administrative matters to raise, I'll ask him to proceed now with his cross-examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have two administrative matters to raise, very important ones, and unless those matters are clarified, I don't think it will be possible for the cross-examination of this witness to continue. But before I do that, I'd like to provide the witness with a set of documents, and I'd like the witness to have the possibility of studying those documents during the break, because I'm not going to use any of those documents before the break. So if he could use that time to look through them, and then we could save time during the cross-examination. There are many documents there. Some of them still have not been translated, but I did provide them on time, I think some three months ago, in fact. Now, the first problem is this: The OTP has not provided me with a statement or the interview of General Zivota Panic, and it was duty-bound to disclose it to me, and this is a violation of Article 21, para 1, 2 and 4(b) and (e) of the Statute. It's a violation of the 68(1) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence and Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The European Court for Human Rights has already had a number of judgements passed, and the view in those judgements is the following: That the procedure in all criminal proceedings must be contradictory, adversary, and guarantee the equality of the parties. That is what is called "the equality of arms" in the judgement by the European Court, and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "Adversarial," interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So that is the basic right. Any failure to disclose any relevant evidence upsets the principle of a fair and efficacious trial. On the basis of 6(1) of the European Convention, it is the duty of the Prosecution to provide the Defence with all relevant evidence and documents that it has in its possession. This right to an adversarial proceedings means that both sides can be informed of each other's evidence and documents and that they can discuss them. And I would like to remind you of Franzepen [phoen] versus Austria, a case in 1991; Hit [phoen] versus Great Britain, 1996; Jasper versus Great Britain, 1995; and so on and so forth, the precedence for that. Now, there is no reason why in this particular trial any restrictions should be applied, nor is the Prosecution -- nor did the Prosecution stress any restrictions in its comments with respect to the questioning and statement of Zivota Panic. Now, since the European Convention on Human Rights protects the interests of the parties and the interests of justice and law at the same time, the parties in the proceedings must be provided with a possibility of stating their views as to whether a document is worthy of their comments and should be used in the proceedings or not. And the functioning of their organs is based on, among other things, the fact that each party can state its views on any document and piece of evidence contained in the file, in the dossier. Now, it is beyond all reasonable doubt that the statement given by General Panic, who was the commander of the 1st Military District, whose authority stretched over Vukovar and to which the 1st Guard's proletarian Division was subordinated, and by the same token the 1st Guards Brigade, Sector South and North, that that is exceptionally relevant and of capitol importance to my defence, as well as the final outcome of this trial in general. I was not given the possibility of becoming acquainted with the contents, and then, with respect to those contents, to be able to question this expert witness, Mr. Theunens, who belongs to the OTP team, Prosecution team. And you saw last time he confirmed that as a member of the Prosecution team, he took part in the questioning of the witness, in the questioning of the suspects, in preparing the witness for testimony, and performed all the tasks that other members of the Prosecution team perform. Now, there is absolutely no equality of arms here, therefore, and I have provided you with two statements which arrived -- which came to my possession yesterday, so I found them in my cell at 5.00 p.m., 5.00 in the afternoon, and I had a visit throughout the day, my family came to visit me, and I was given that at 5.00 in the afternoon. Perhaps the Detention Unit received the material earlier on, but I could not provide a translation on time. It is the statement by Lieutenant Colonel Vidoje Mijailovic and the statement by Colonel Mijo Milosevic as well. And they are witnesses to the fact that on the 27th of October, 2002, in Pancevo, at an assembly of the association of former members of the 51st Mechanised Brigade, whose headquarters is in Pancevo, and whose commander was once a long time ago, General Zivota Panic. They talked to General Panic, and I would like to read out to you just the most relevant portions of those statements, and you have in front of you the statements in their entirety, certified in the Municipal Court of Pancevo, on the 25th of February, 2008. That is to say, they were certified yesterday. Lieutenant Colonel Vidoje Mijailovic and Colonel Mijo Milosevic saw the footage, the video, of the examination-in-chief of this witness and my insistence on the statement and the text of the questioning and interview of Zivota Panic, and that is what motivated them to contact a member of the team. Assisting in my Defence, a lawyer, Pete Vijojic [phoen], was contacted, and they offered these statements to him. Lieutenant Colonel Vidoje Mijailovic says here that on that occasion, Zivota Panic complained to him and said that he had a lot of very serious problems in his life created by the investigators of The Hague Tribunal, that he was frightened for his life and the life of his children, and said that The Hague interpreters questioned him for 12 days, 10 hours continuously and exerted pressure upon him, that they blackmailed and threatened him that they would raise an indictment against him unless he agreed to be a witness of the Prosecution before The Hague Tribunal unless he stated what The Hague investigators demanded that he said, and that during the questioning, many of the documents were put to him, whereas he had never heard of any of those documents before or knew what their contents were. And that was what the greatest trouble was, as far as he was concerned, because he was asked to confirm the documents, and unless he did so The Hague Prosecution would raise an indictment against him for war crimes. As Lieutenant Colonel Mijailovic says, General Panic also told him that The Hague investigators forced him to sign a statement. And now my comment to that: The statement exists. There are two witnesses that confirm that Zivota Panic told him that he had signed the statement.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter's correction, The Hague "investigators," not The Hague "interpreters" earlier on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Mr. Seselj. I'm listening to you with great interest, but one fellow judge has a question about the possible link between the cross-examination of this witness and General Panic. Is there a link? Could you please tell us about this, and then you can proceed with your comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Gentlemen, Judges, I'm going to disclose a little secret that the Prosecution did not know about. In August 2004, along with a certification, certification number 6, and you can ask the Prosecutor for the entire contents of the Document Number 6, the Prosecution gave me a short resume -- supplied me with a short resume of General Panic's statement. And as far as I'm concerned, it is absolutely exculpatory, and I have to put that statement to this witness during the cross-examination. At the status conference on the 4th of October, 2004, I demanded the Pre-Trial Judge Agius at the time to request the Prosecution to provide me with the statement in its entirety. Agius' response was, and you can see the transcript from that 4th of October, 2004, status conference, that the Judges of the pre-trial Chamber did not receive that exculpatory -- do not receive the exculpatory material that the Prosecution is duty-bound to disclose to me. And then he asked that I make the request in writing. After a certain amount of time, I did ask to receive this in writing, but the Prosecution never provided me with Zivota Panic's statement. Zivota Panic says in that statement that all the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party were within the composition of the JNA units, that not a single one was suspected of war crimes, that they were disciplined, and he claims that the White Eagles, Beli Orlovi were never within the composition of the JNA, and so on and so forth. So these are statements he makes in that statement of his, so General Zivota Panic's statement is extremely important to me, so that the witness -- I can put certain parts of that statement to the witness. He's an expert witness and a member of the Prosecution team, so I'd like to hear his views on that statement. I'd also like to finish quoting from the statements. I have almost finished Vidoje Mijailovic's statement, and then I would like to go on very, very briefly from Colonel Mijo Milosevic's statement, a short excerpt there, and then I would like to ask the Trial Chamber to take certain steps in that regard. General Zivota Panic also said to Vidoje Mijailovic, as it says here in the statement, that The Hague investigators forced him to sign a statement which they compiled, but that he would never recognise that statement as being his own. And the statement that he signed, he was never provided with, and that he's very sorry that he hasn't got a copy of that statement of his so that he could show us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you're going too fast. Can you please repeat what you've just said, but please do so more slowly, because we want to understand exactly what you're saying. So please start again, but slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The sense of what I'm quoting now is something additional, that is to say, that in the statement something it says that Zivota Panic did not wish to have contained in the statement, but after the terrible pressures exerted upon on him, he signed everything without reading the statement. And he said that according to the testimony of Lieutenant Colonel Vidoje Mijailovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're talking about the statement signed by General Panic, whereas last week the Prosecutor told us that there is no document, there has never been such document. That's why I was asking you to repeat what you just said very slowly, in order for us to be aware of the matter at hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] President, I am insisting on the fact that General Panic's statement does exist, that's what I maintain, and that the Prosecution is attempting to hide it. Lieutenant Colonel Mijailovic says that Zivota Panic also told him the following: That The Hague investigators forced him to sign a statement which they compiled, but that he would never recognise that statement as being his own, and that that statement, the one he signed, was never given to him, and that he is very sorry that he hasn't got a copy of that statement of his in order to be able to show us all the troubles he had to go through and all the terror exerted against him, and pressure, and blackmail. That's what Vidoje Mijailovic says. General Panic also told him that The Hague investigators offered him every form of assistance, beginning with monetary assistance and other benefits. And they said that they would not be raising an indictment against him if he agreed to be a Prosecution witness. He also told him that the whole time these threats and pressures were being exerted against him, he refused to testify falsely and did not accept any other benefits of enticements. And then he stresses that as a heart patient, he was forced to sign the statement under duress and under threat, and that during these 12 days of abuse, they broke him down and he could take it no longer. Now, you know that immediately after that, Judges, Zivota Panic did in fact have a heart attack and died of that heart attack. Now, according to the statement made by Colonel Mijo Milosevic, given also on Monday, the 25th of February, that is to say, yesterday, Colonel Milosevic describes that same meeting of officers of former members of the 51st Mechanised Brigade in Pancevo and says the following: "During the conversation with General Zivota Panic, I saw that he was very much concerned and worried, and he complained that The Hague investigators questioned him for a full 12 days continuously. And that The Hague investigators were creating major problems for him because they asked him to be a Prosecution witness of The Hague Tribunal and that they gave him a very hard time, but that he refused, nonetheless, to be a Prosecution witness, and that he wasn't going to make false testimony against the military and political leadership of our country, of our state." General Panic also said that The Hague investigators exerted pressure on him and that they tried to blackmail him and threaten him that they would raise an indictment against him if he failed to agree to be a Prosecution witness, and he refused to cooperate. Now, a copy of his statement was not provided to him. And now Colonel Milosevic describes here who also was present, and they were General Enes Taso, Colonel Zoran Jovanovic, Lieutenant Colonel Milenko Lukic. He was there as well as others. Therefore, I have two pieces of evidence that a statement exists by General Zivota Panic in the Prosecution, they have it. The third piece of evidence is confirmation number 6 of the Prosecution. So before you make a ruling, would you please request that the Prosecution provides you with confirmation or certification number 6 and the summary of certain statements that they disclosed to me with that, and you will find a summary of the statement made by General Zivota Panic. There are two. They sent that to me pursuant to Rule 68. Now, Zivota Panic -- they exerted pressure on Zivota Panic to be a false witness in the Milosevic trial, to begin with, but along the way he mentioned the role of the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party and, as far as I'm concerned, gave an absolutely exculpatory statement. Now, the Prosecution didn't take that into account at the time because the pressure was directed against Milosevic -- for him to testify against Milosevic. We're dealing here with 2001, when the Milosevic trial was still ongoing, and they weren't even thinking about raising an indictment against me at that time. So that is why this slipped in, and it's completely exculpatory where I'm concerned. So, please, would you request that the Prosecution provide me with a statement of Zivota Panic straightaway and the transcript of his interview and questioning. I have nowhere else that I can use this except during the cross-examination of expert witness Mr. Theunens here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Let me summarise, and then I'll ask the Prosecution to tell us what their position is. Everything started the following way: Last week, during examination-in-chief, mention was made at one time of the role played by General Panic at the time of the Vukovar events, and let me remind you that the Vukovar events are pleaded in the indictment. Therefore, General Panic at the time was at the head of the 1st Military District, and Vukovar was located within the 1st Military District. Then the accused, Mr. Seselj, when raising an objection, stated that he had in his possession a summary of the statement made by General Panic that, according to Mr. Seselj, demonstrates that Mr. Panic had made a written statement to the OTP. Mr. Seselj told us that this is certificate number 6. Having said that, I have to go back even further in time to the pre-trial stage, and my two fellow Judges did not take part in that stage and they might not be aware of some information, if they have any time to delve in the hundreds of pages of documents produced by the pre-trial stage that lasted for a very long time. At some point during the pre-trial stage, the accused told us that he had been informed that there were 207.000 pages of exculpatory evidence. According to the Rules, he demanded to be provided with these documents. Following this request, I told Ms. Dahl that she had to do everything for the accused to receive as many pages as possible of these documents, but I also said that in order to facilitate this on the side of the Prosecution, the accused could give key words to the Prosecution for the Prosecution to then conduct a document search. That was done, and I understand that 3.000 pages were disclosed to the accused, thanks to these key word searches. It appears that according to the accused, everything General Panic said comes under Rule 67, and that under other Rules the accused would like to receive the written statement made by General Panic, and it is the duty of the Prosecution to disclose this document. Otherwise, they might receive very serious sanctions. Because of this, last week I solemnly asked the Prosecution to conduct a thorough check and to check that there had never been any written and signed statement. And last week, at the end of last week, the OTP told us here, in this courtroom, that General Panic had been heard or questioned as a suspect, but that no written and signed statement had been produced. Since that time, since the end of last week, we've seen two documents appear from two colonels. We've received the statements in B/C/S, without a translation, but allegedly, according to these two men, General Panic, before he died, because apparently he had a heart attack, he apparently stated that the Office of the Prosecutor, after 12 days of interviews, questioning, had him sign or purportedly had him sign a document, and that this document exists, there is such a document, since General Panic allegedly told of this to these two colonels who certify this fact or attest to that fact in this document. What is the exact position now? Mr. Marcussen, can you please shed some light on this for us?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Good morning. To deal with the last issue first, the issue of the material we have from General Panic, now, we're still looking into this after the discussions that took place last week, but the status is still today, as far as I know, that we don't have anything -- any written statements signed by Panic. We have the recordings of the suspect interview. We have a transcript from a documentary prepared by the BBC. That transcript was -- has been given initials by General Panic whereby he adopts what is in the transcripts. And then we appear to have the August document, which I haven't looked at but I just saw on the screen now, which appears to be summaries, a notification to the accused of some of the contents of the suspect interview of Mr. Panic. Now, the accused is presenting two statements from people who say that Panic has said that he has signed a statement. Now, whether that is correct, whether Panic has said that, whether he -- why he might have said that, I don't know. I would like to -- again, I was given some time, and I'm grateful for that, to look into this. I'd like a bit more time to make sure we've turned over all the pages that we need to turn in the OTP to determine whether there exists a statement, but we have so far not been able to find anything and we have been looking for this material. So at this stage, I think there's confusion maybe on the part of the accused because of these different types of written material related to Panic's statement. But as I stand here today, as far as I know, there is no written statement. We'll continue to look into it, and I'll report back before this witness has finished his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've understood. This certificate, acknowledgment of receipt number 6, is a summary that the accused has in his possession. According to you, was this summary prepared on the basis of this suspect interview which we can see in the DVD, or was it prepared on the basis of a written statement which you cannot find?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I'm having the particular document printed and brought down to me so I can take a look at it. I would think that it is done based on the recorded suspect interview. I see -- we would have disclosed, if we felt necessary, the statement itself or excerpts from it, if that existed. So just from the nature of this kind of a document, I would think it's done exactly because we don't have a statement but because we have a recording which is a less-handy document to work with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now, the other question I have for you: General Panic, who commanded the 1st Military District, normally speaking, if crimes had been committed in Vukovar, the question could have arisen; in other words, he could have been involved in these crimes, either under Article 7(1) or 7(3) of the Statute. Seemingly, General Panic was not prosecuted in any way. Nonetheless, all the information collected by the OTP on General Panic should have been disclosed to the accused, because the accused needs to rebut what happened in Vukovar. Therefore, he needs to -- also according to him, this is exculpatory material. He should have been handed over, in his own language, the transcript of the DVD. So does the Prosecution have any intention of having this translated and have any intention of disclosing this to him, because he has asked this for two reasons; under Article 67, but also under Article 68 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, what the accused considers to be exculpatory in nature is, from what he's saying, the fact that volunteers were resubordinated to the JNA while they were in Vukovar. That is also the Prosecution's case. The accused is presenting a number of issues as if they were exculpatory, as if it's inconsistent with the Office of the Prosecution's allegations in the case, but they're actually not. Mr. Theunens gave evidence about the resubordination of volunteers to the JNA during the Vukovar campaign and during other periods in time that are relevant to the indictment. So this is not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marcussen, I am not going to give you any legal -- a legal lesson here, but just a few reminders, in legal terms, that we understand what's at stake here. If crimes were committed in Vukovar, the question is: Who committed these crimes? If it so happens that the people who committed the crimes were members of the army subordinated to the JNA, then this comes under the responsibility of the JNA. And what about the responsibility of the accused? In the indictment, the accused is charged under Article 7(1) in all its forms, and, amongst others, he's charged for his role in the JCE. Now, if we take JCE and its third form, in other words, if crimes were committed by the JNA under form 3 of the JCE, he could be held liable for these crimes, but if there is no joint criminal enterprise because the Prosecution would be unable to prove that such a joint criminal enterprise existed, then Mr. Seselj would be held liable for the other forms mentioned in Article 7(1); did he order, did he plan, and so on and so forth. So he can quite legitimately feel that he needs to know whether these crimes were committed by perpetrators under the control of the JNA, and he had no authority over the JNA. He had no authority to order, to plan and so on and so forth. That is why it is so important to know whether Mr. Panic said what he might have said. So this must be disclosed to him. You draw other conclusions, because you feel that this is not exculpatory material and therefore you need not disclose this to him, but his point of view is different. This is what the whole question hinges on. So you did disclose some of the material because the DVD has been sent to him. The decision had been taken. In other words, when we are talking about exculpatory material, the exculpatory material should be disclosed in a hard copy form and in his own language so that he can use it. So what do you have to say to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour, I don't think there's any disagreement about neither the scope of Rule 68 nor the potential significance of Panic's interview. We are in the process of reviewing again the Panic interviews, as he was interviewed for a number of days, so we are having people looking at the recordings to determine whether or not there is any material that falls within Rule 68. The obligation of compliance with Rule 68 is, on the Prosecution, we're fully aware of our obligation under that Rule, and we take it very seriously. Now, it is not because the accused states that something is exculpatory, in his view, that it falls within Rule 68. There's no dispute that the material is relevant. We have tried to disclose the material to the accused on Thursday or Friday, when we tried to give him the DVD with the recordings to enable him to review the material. If something is -- falls within Rule 68, Your Honours have ruled that we need to provide the material in written form to the accused, and we will do so if we determine that there is exculpatory material in the interview. Now, the process of transcribing I think it's 43 hours of interview or something like that is not something that can be done overnight, and if we have to do that once we have reviewed the material, we will do it. There's no -- there's no dispute there. But as I said, there is an issue about what is actually exculpatory in this case. Now, if Your Honours order us to provide a transcription of this, then of course we will comply, but what we're doing is we're adopting the Rules as they have been understood so far in this case, namely, that Rule 68(b) material or Rule 68(2) material is provided to the accused in the form that we have it, and 68 material and statements of witnesses and so on and so forth are provided in hard copy in the language of the accused. So we are in the process of doing this, and I have been given notification of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've understood, Mr. Marcussen, what you're saying. I have another question. You said that these 12 interviews with Mr. Panic amount to 43 hours. Forty-three hours -- four hours is approximately 100 pages, so 43 hours, you would have a thousand pages of transcript. So these 43 hours and these thousand pages, would these be included in the 207.000 documents which the accused has been notified of or would this not be part of that batch of documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I would suspect that it does not, the reason being the following: The big number of pages that we're talking about originates from various collections of material that the Office of the Prosecutor has received during various times, so it is documentary evidence, whereas what we're talking about here is a suspect interview, so that would fall within a separate collection of material, if you want.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So let me sum up your position. I shall give the floor back to Mr. Seselj. A, there is no written statement, but you are still checking this out. B, you confirm that there have been 12 suspect interviews of 43 hours, which amount to hundreds of pages, and you will do all you can to disclose this to Mr. Seselj under Rule 68. That is your position. I've understood you correctly, haven't I, Mr. Seselj, unless you would like to add something, Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I do feel it necessary to refute the allegations of pressure put on the witness during the interviews. If Your Honours would like, we are happy to provide a recording of the suspect interviews so you can see for yourself how the interviews took place. There is just absolutely no basis for the allegations that come up now about pressure against these witnesses. Of course, those feed into a number of other allegations of the same nature. These will be dealt with later, if the Trial Chamber find it necessary, pursuant to the order, but I do find it necessary to strongly refute these allegations. They are misplaced, there is no basis for them. And I find it quite disturbing that we continue have these sort of allegations sort of the on the fly in court, those statements that come in last minute and it being addressed in this matter. But we will get back to this, I suspect, later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I must point out two things. Firstly, you mentioned key words on the basis of which the OTP should identify potential exculpatory material and disclose it to me. They disclosed to me potentially exculpatory material on the basis of only three key words: Arkan's Tigers, Yellow Wasps, White Eagles. They avoided disclosing to me potentially exculpatory material for the key word "Serbian Guard," and those are the four key words, if I remember correctly, which you mentioned, and I think I do remember correctly. However, the two most important key words, when identifying potentially exculpatory material, must be my name and "Serb Radical Party," so they should have disclosed to me all the material they have available where my name is mentioned, even if only once, or the name of the Serbian Radical Party. I think that is the very minimum of potential exculpatory material. Secondly, the Prosecutor has insisted more than once here that they do not know whether Zivota Panic's statement is exculpatory for me, that it is only my claim. Judges, sirs, I am not claiming that the statement or the interview of General Zivota Panic is potentially exculpatory for me. It was the Prosecution that established this on the 19th of August, 2004, with receipt number 26. They disclosed to me 23 various summaries under Rule 68(1). These are different statements by different people, given under different circumstances. Under number 14 was a summary of the statement of General Zivota Panic. The summary of General Zivota Panic's statement was then given to me in eight points. You don't imagine that someone in the OTP viewed all those videos again and then drew up those eight points. The summary was based on a statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... Right away, Mr. Seselj. Mr. Marcussen, Mr. Seselj, I didn't mention this a few moments ago, but during the status conference, in the presence of Judge Agius, the issue had been officially addressed, and Judge Agius had quite rightly said that these documents should be disclosed by the Prosecution to Mr. Seselj, and had therefore at the time asked the Prosecution to disclose to Mr. Seselj all these documents. Mr. Seselj has just told us that on the 19th of August, 2004, there were 23 summaries which were disclosed to him. This includes certificate number 6, which means that as of 2004 onwards, as far as the Prosecution is concerned, the summary may contain exculpatory material. In addition, we had agreed with Mrs. Dahl that by using key words, she was to search in all the documents anything pertaining to the Yellow Wasps, about Seselj's name, and conduct a search with those words, including the Serbian Radical Party. Now, these 43 hours of interview with General Panic which you mentioned, well, normally speaking, if you're using this software package, you should be able to find mention of Mr. Seselj, if General Panic mentioned him. I'm sure he mentioned him by the mere fact that Mr. Seselj came to Vukovar, and therefore one can be more or less sure that he did mention his name. Did he mention the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party? That, I don't know. So, Mr. Marcussen, before giving the floor back to Mr. Seselj, as far as these 23 summaries are concerned, those that have been disclosed under Rule 68, and certificate number 6 is part of these documents, this happened as early as August of 2004. This is where the Prosecution felt that there was exculpatory material in this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Two points, Your Honours. First, as to the ability of search engines to pick up information within Panic's interview, the problem is that when a file is -- when we have on the audio recording -- when we do a search for words in documents, it doesn't capture an audio recording. The search engine cannot search in an audio file. They search for words in written documents. So the search wouldn't have come up in that kind of a context. I have just received receipt number 6 and the summary, and indeed there is mention of --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may intervene, Mr. President. As the Prosecutor has now got receipt number 6, let him first find item 14 and read point 1 of the summary of Zivota Panic's statement in its entirety. It's very brief, just a few sentences. Please let him do this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It would have been interesting for the Trial Chamber to have this certificate, certificate number 6, but you've just confirmed, haven't you, that Mr. Seselj is mentioned in this document, and Mr. Seselj would like you to read this out to us, the item.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I take slight issue with the fact that the accused is cutting me off while I'm making my submissions and trying to direct what I should be doing later on. I would like to provide Your Honours with a copy of receipt number 6. So, Your Honours, I was explaining why a search for words do not pick up the contents of an audio or video recording. Now, as I said, on the second point, the receipt number 10 -- sorry, receipt number 6, indeed, on the 19th of August, 2004, there was a disclosure which was qualified as a Rule 68 disclosure and which provides the summary of -- yeah, I believe there were eight items that were considered to be potentially exculpatory, falling within Rule 68 at the time. So this information was provided at the time to the accused, so he was -- he was told what material was considered falling within Rule 68 at the time. I mean, I think -- I appreciate that, later on, that the scene for disclosure of this kind of material has changed so that the format in which the disclosure should take place has changed, so that it is being required now that it provides material in hard copy. In August of 2004, that was not the requirement. But I think the important point is that the material that the accused should have has been given to him since August. And, again, the point that the accused is making based on this material, namely, that as SRS/SCP volunteers were operating under the command of the JNA, well, that is not in dispute by the Office of the Prosecutor. That is, indeed, what we're saying. The case is in -- well, an additional issue as to whether or not the accused also had control at the same time over his volunteers, and we've heard evidence about that, and there would be more evidence about that during the case. Now, as I said, the Office of the Prosecutor can transcribe the entire interview. That will take whatever time it will take, but we can undertake to do that. But it's not something that can be done overnight. The accused is refusing to work with the audio recordings, and that sort of blocks us. The Office of the Prosecutor does not -- we don't have a transcript of the English version. We're producing material here for the benefit of the accused that we don't even have ourselves. We are also in the process of doing transcripts of the B/C/S hearings where our -- the witnesses that are going to be called testified, so there are many transcription processes in motion at this time, and we can put this into the pipeline as well or we can try to identify the portions of Panic's interview that are covered by the eight points in receipt number 10 and transcribe those relevant parts for the accused. But I think this receipt gives the accused notice of the relevant bits of the interview with General Panic. And for the purpose of the accused's cross-examination of Mr. Panic, he can put the propositions he wants to put to the witness. He doesn't need a statement from Panic to put these propositions to the witness. So I don't see why this issue should in any way impede the accused's possibility to carry out his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, you can also look at the transcript of the status conference of the 14th of October, 2004, and on several occasions after that I insisted that the statement of General Zivota Panic be disclosed to me in full. At that time, I did not even know that General Panic had been interviewed as a suspect and that there had to be a video recording. In 2004, no one offered that video to me. A summary is made based on a statement, not based on a video recording. Imagine someone in the OTP, whenever it is required, has to view the entire video, take notes, and then draw up a summary based on those notes. For the sake of the public, if need be, I can read it, just item 1 out of these eight items of the summary of Zivota Panic's interview. Maybe the Prosecution is ashamed of this, so let me read it out in item number 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which item would you like to highlight?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just item 1 of the summary of General Zivota Panic's statement or interview. Just let me read it, unless there is an objection by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Marcussen. On page 2, this is the item we are interested --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: The first item reads: "Chetniks who came to the combat area (Vukovar and its vicinity) placed themselves under the JNA command and could therefore not be considered paramilitaries anymore. They carried out tasks given to them by OG --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecutor read more slowly for the interpreters, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: My apologies. "They carried out the tasks given to them by OG South. Seselj sent one or two groups of Chetniks to Vukovar. They were integrated in operative units in OG South, but remained together as a distinct group within the JNA units, wearing JNA insignia. Panic said that he ordered Mrksic to equip and clothe SRS volunteers who came to OG South (timing is not available). There were never any reports about any wrongdoing by these volunteers. White Eagles were never integrated into the armed forces because they were criminals. Panic is adamant that during the operations in Croatia, there were never any paramilitary groups included in the OG." If I may add a comment, I think this is fairly consistent with what the evidence of Mr. Theunens has been so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Seselj, we have to conclude on the matter. The Prosecutor will do what it should and provide you, as soon as it can, because this will take some time, with what General Panic has said. The Prosecutor is right in this. In light of the summary, you are able to cross-examine the witness on these matters. This is the first point you wanted to raise. What was the second point you wanted to raise?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it may be poor interpretation, but in the summary it says that General Zivota Panic ordered General Mrksic to arm the volunteers of the Serb Radical Party. That was not said in the interpretation, and that General Panic -- there was something else I observed, but now it escapes me -- that these volunteers carried out the tasks of Operative Group South. And in footnote number 1, it says that General Panic used the expression "Seselj's men, sympathisers of the Serbian Radical Party" and "adherents of the Serbian Radical Party." He used those terms to identify those volunteers, so that it is clear to General Panic also that Seselj's men were a specific group and that not all Chetniks could be considered to be Seselj's men. What I wanted to say was the following: My rights have not been respected here. Of course, I can cross-examine this witness even if not a single document is disclosed to me, and I do not want to interrupt these proceedings for any reason, but it is my right to openly brand the unlawful behaviour of the OTP each time it occurs. In my view, General Panic's interview is a document under Rule 68(1). I have the right to have that document disclosed to me, and it has not been disclosed. This witness would have been an ideal opportunity to make use of that material in my cross-examination, but I cannot use a summary of the statement in my cross-examination, and I will not use it. Let me say one more thing. There is not a shred of evidence that the OTP, as of Thursday last week, started transcribing the interviews of Zivota Panic. They haven't even started doing it. They think they can avoid it. That's the problem I'm facing. Well, now, to give you a specific example, I happened to have an opportunity to unmask the entire background of all this. Imagine how many similar instances there are that I know nothing about. What is happening now is the pattern of behaviour of the OTP over the past five years. Documents are being concealed from me. I am being given the documents drop by drop. Less relevant documents are disclosed to me, while key documents are concealed. These are all the facts I have to face. Of course, I'm aware of these facts, and in spite of these facts, I will continue to defend myself, I will continue my cross-examination of this witness. But I think that by agglomerating all this evidence of the unlawful behaviour of the OTP, I will bring about a situation where the Chamber will have to take measures. We have not had a single witness here without procedural problems cropping up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Before I give the floor back to Mr. Marcussen, I would like, on my own behalf, to make a significant comment. Rule 48 -- Rule 68, I'd like to read this Rule: "(i). The Prosecutor shall as soon practicable disclose to the Defence any material which in the actual knowledge of the Prosecutor may suggest the innocence or mitigate the guilt of the accused." And we have another significant comment under (ii). I quote: "The Prosecutor shall make available to the Defence in electronic form a collection of relevant material held by the Prosecutor, together with the appropriate computer software with which the Defence can search such collections electronically." So since a lawyer may speak French or English, as a counsel he may receive the documents in either languages, but when we have an accused who defends himself, and this is the case with Mr. Seselj, I interpret (i) as meaning he must have receive, in hard copy and in his language, everything that is related in paragraph (i). Now, anything related to electronic searches, let's assume, for example, that Mr. Seselj would like to search for further material, this is another issue. That's my interpretation. But if we talk of General Panic, commander of a military district involved in the Vukovar events, then, as far as I'm concerned, I think that the hearing of Mr. Panic is related to Rule 68(i), and therefore the transcript must be disclosed to the accused on hard copy in his language. Otherwise, the equality of arms is not observed. This is as much as I wanted to say in order for this to be on the transcript. Mr. Marcussen, do you have anything to add?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: For the record, since the Presiding Judge has offered his view, that I might have the same view, but I'm unable to make any final determination of the issue of whether the statement by Panic -- or the interview with Panic does or does not come under Rule 68 until I've seen the interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would also like to add something, considering the views of the Presiding Judge, of course. But up to now, the Chamber had never made such a decision, so this also explains and justifies the action of the Prosecution, who have not disclosed the material up to now, all of the exculpatory material, at least as considered by the accused. So I would like to add one comment, which is as follows. It is for the Prosecution to check out in order to see whether or not an exculpatory document is such, and of course if the Prosecution conceals any materials, their responsibility may be subject to punishment by the Chamber. But in any case, it is the responsibility of the Prosecution to check out in order to see whether such material exists.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. As for the President's interpretation of Rule 68, (i) and (ii), I believe that has been formalised in a decision that has been issued about the mode of disclosure, and we are complying with that decision when we disclose material to the accused. We have -- in 2004, the Office of the Prosecutor already disclosed, as potentially exculpatory, the information that is included in receipt number 6. As it is with these things, when reference is made to Article 68, it's difficult to know whether things are within Rule 68(i) or (ii), so whether it's relevant or exculpatory. It is also difficult to make these sort of determinations when there appear to be different views about what is exculpatory; for example, the issue of whether or not it is exculpatory that the volunteers were subordinated through the JNA. As I said, we are in the process of reviewing the whole set of interviews once again and are trying to find exculpatory material. Now, I must say that I took the President's statement as being an order to us that we should transcribe the testimony, and if -- should transcribe the suspect interview, and if that is the view, then of course we do as we're ordered to. We're certainly not trying to hide anything, and I guess that's the bottom line of what I'm trying to say. We provided this material to the accused. We informed him of the contents of the suspect interview. We did so in 2004. We're prepared to provide him the audio recordings. He is refusing to receive them. He has the exact material we have. If we are directed to transcribe this whole thing to him, we will do that. And all I'm saying with respect to the timing of that is, it's not going to be something that can be done overnight, in light of the volume, and it has to be fed into the pipeline of material that we are in the process of transcribing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a second, because I'd like to complete what I said, given what my colleague Judge Lattanzi just said. I would like the legal officer to find for the Chamber the transcriptions of all the decisions in order to see what is relevant to electronic disclosure. In addition to this, I would like to say that I share the views of Judge Harhoff as to the relevance of what is or is not exculpatory. But in order to determine on this issue, we need to see the interview of General Panic, which we haven't seen yet. There may be exculpatory elements in that interview, but in order to decide, we need to have the document. So before the Prosecution starts anything, I'm telling the OTP that they should disclose electronically General Panic's statement to the Chamber. The Chamber will review that statement and then will tell the Prosecution whether or not there should be a disclosure on hard copy to the accused. But in any case, there is already an existing major material problem, which is that regarding the 1.000 pages, it is quite obvious that 1.000 pages are not relevant to Vukovar. So within these 1.000 pages, the Chamber should know exactly what are the relevant passages as to Vukovar. But in order to determine this, the Chamber needs to have the document. So, please, give us first the DVD, and then we'll tell you what are the passages that should be disclosed to the accused if the Chamber are unanimous. If the Chamber are not unanimous, then a decision will be made with possibly individual dissenting opinions. And if need be, the issue may be submitted to the Appeals Chamber. So that's what I meant to say. We have spent over an hour and 15 minutes on these procedure issues. Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, in my opinion and as far as I see it, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, neither you nor your colleagues are looking at the relevance of evidence -- or, rather, when -- or, rather, you have to attach weight to the various evidence. Now, according to the Rules, the OTP assesses which document in their possession can be potentially exculpatory. The Prosecutor has already made that assessment. He made it in 2004. So they don't have to go into a reevaluation of that now. That would be misplaced. Secondly, I insisted here that only point 1 of the summary be read out. There are seven other points, because it's an eight-point statement, which are also relevant for my defence because they relate to the alleged joint criminal enterprise. Now, this joint criminal enterprise links me up to Slobodan Milosevic and all the rest, everything else. So it's not only when General Panic mentions my name or the members of the Serbian Radical Party which is relevant. Other things are relevant, too, when he speaks of the role of Milosevic and Kadijevic and Adzic, and a whole series of other individuals who were proclaimed in different indictments raised by the Prosecution for having been participants in the joint criminal enterprise at top level, and I find it an honour to find my name among them there. Don't misunderstand me. It's an honour for me to be quoted at that top level and qualified as a participant at this imagined joint criminal enterprise. It strengthens my historical role and worth. However, the Prosecution must provide me with all the information which can challenge the existence of the joint criminal enterprise itself, and so I'm opposed to the fact that the Trial Chamber can view all these videos and footage and then mark which part is relevant for my defence and which is not. The entire footage must be transcribed on paper so that then I can assess what can be useful to me and what is not useful, because if you are the filter, if you are put in the role of the filter in assessing all this, then the Trial Chamber runs the risk of being an appendage to the OTP, that you have to say, "This is necessary, this is not necessary." I understand what the OTP wishes to achieve, but I don't think that the Trial Chamber can allow itself to play that role. The minimum of minimum requirements as far as exculpatory material is concerned are the documents, all the documents where my name is mentioned and the Serbian Radical Party is mentioned, because all that can potentially be exculpatory for me. So that is the minimum of documents that the Prosecution must disclose to me on paper and in the Serbian language. And I drew your attention on many occasions, Mr. President, that the OTP is just not ready to go ahead with this trial. I have done nothing for four or five years, and this is the beginning of my sixth year, and on Sunday I celebrated five years of imprisonment in The Hague with my fellow prisoners. This is now my sixth year. So I never slowed down these proceedings, so my struggle for my elementary rights cannot be considered that I'm slowing down the process. And I'm fighting for my basic rights, and I'm telling you that that was an order, as far as I'm concerned, and it is proper in this particular instance. It is my right to have the entire interview of Zivota Panic put down on paper and the summary on the basis of the statement because -- and the entire statement, because the summary is based on the statement, not on the interview. Picture the following situation: When the Prosecution talks to someone who is a potential subject and talks to that person for 10 or 15 days, they record all the proceedings, and any time they need it in some other trial, then they look through -- would have to look through all this recording and then make a summary on the basis of their notes when they review the material, review the recording. That is just not done. It would be stupid. What they have is a statement. The statement represents the document which is again compiled by the Prosecution on the basis of the questioning, interview. You see, a statement is a form of a summary or precis of the questioning or interview. And then they give me the summary of the statement, because in the summary the Prosecution refers to Zivota Panic in the third person, not the first person, it does not say: "I, Zivota Panic, say such-and-such." It is the Prosecutor who in the summary describes what he happened to notice from the statement made by Zivota Panic which could be potentially exculpatory for me. And the other seven points are highly relevant, because it is on the basis of the other seven points and the material on the basis of which those points were constituted that I have the possibility of refuting the whole question of the existence of the joint criminal enterprise, and that's not something that's impossible. Let me remind you that in Mrksic, Sljivancanin and Radic, the joint criminal enterprise concept fell through. The Trial Chamber rejected it, rejected the fact that any joint criminal enterprise existed in Vukovar at all. So if General Mrksic, Colonel Sljivancanin and Major Radic were not members of the JCE in Vukovar, then how can I be a member of it? Then I would be there on my own, as a single member, just one member of the JCE. So these are very complicated matters, and for us to be able to deal with the matters in a rational fashion, all the relevant documents must be provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is another issue. In order to conclude on material disclosure, I would like to remind everyone that a decision was made on June the 7th by myself in the framework of the Pre-Trial Chamber following motion 249 regarding document disclosure. The decision has ten pages, and I quote: "Orders the Prosecution to disclose as soon as possible, on hard copy and in a language understood by the accused, the documents mentioned under item I." Rule 68, item I. And so a decision was made, and on November the 5th, 2007, another decision was made by the Chamber whose title is: "Second decision regarding the obligation of the Prosecution resulting from the Rules of Procedure and Evidence." I quote: "The Chamber orders the Prosecution to disclose as soon as possible in hard copy and in a language understood by the accused the 3.000 documents about -- identified by the OTP, thanks to the key words given by the accused." End of quotation. So Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I'm slightly concerned about the way the allegations are now spiraling from the Office of the Prosecutor to potential issues with the Chamber and things like that. I was going to offer that we, within -- it will take us two or three weeks to do, but that we simply transcribe this whole set of interviews. The interviews were done in B/C/S and in English, so Panic speaking in his language is translated, OTP members or staff members speak in English, there's translations back and forth. The accused could have reviewed this with his more than 20 assistants had he wanted to. I am strongly of the belief that we're not hiding anything. It is, to be fair, very difficult to understand why the accused insists on proceeding in this manner, but in light of the way the allegations have been made at the moment, I think the most prudent for all of us is that the Prosecution take on the burden and transcribe this thing and provide it to the accused on this particular occasion. We're not going to continue to do this at the request of the accused in all future cases, but in this particular case, we will undertake to do that to put an end to this matter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So for everybody to be clear on that, a decision was made by the Chamber according to which the Prosecution had to disclose the 3.000 documents identified with the key words. So this is not put into question by the Chamber. The only new element today is anything related to Panic, because apparently the Panic transcripts are not part of these 3.000 documents. So the Chamber may well understand that Mr. Seselj insists on receiving the Panic transcripts on hard copy and in his language. The Chamber, therefore, will have to make a decision on Mr. Seselj's request, and we can make that decision only when we are informed and aware of what Mr. Panic said, because there's no use asking you to have 3.000 pages translated if there's no interest for the Chamber. So we'll see the transcripts and make a decision afterwards. Now, the time of the break has arrived, three minutes before the break. Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. President, I'd like to use those three minutes, not to take up more of your time, so that we can start off with the cross-examination after it straight away. But on Thursday, I understood that the Prosecutor asked that the remaining documents from the register, from the file, which he wasn't able to use during the examination-in-chief of the witness to be included in the exhibits, and then I was opposed to that. Now, over the weekend, or, rather, yesterday, on the 25th of February, I received a much more extensive list of documents which the Prosecution would like to tender. Now, this list reminds me of the November list. I wasn't able to establish whether it is coincides exactly. I think some amendments have been made. Now, I'm not challenging the right of the Prosecutor to tender these documents and the Trial Chamber to admit them outside the examination-in-chief or cross-examination of the witness, but I consider that with respect to each of these documents, we have at least -- I have to say at least "yes" or "no" in the courtroom, I have to state my views, because for each of these documents it must be recorded that it was put forward and tendered, and whether it was just marked for identification or admitted into evidence, and not to have me state my views to all this in writing. If I were to have to give written views, then we could have the whole proceedings and trial conducted in written fashion. I write what I want to say, put down on paper what I want to say. The Prosecution puts in writing what it wants to say and so on. So I would like to state my views on each of these documents, and I can tell you in advance that I would agree to -- or rather, I would agree to two-thirds of the documents, that they be admitted, especially where it comes to excerpts from my books, but there are certain documents that can't be admitted into evidence directly. They have to be put to certain witnesses and we have to discuss the relevance and authenticity of these documents. So I would like to ask you that you set aside one day - you don't have to hurry - in which the Prosecutor would submit all the documents that it wants to have directly admitted, and then we can take it document by document and I can state my views on each of the documents. It is a large number of documents, and we can't just have them admitted without previously discussing them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, the Prosecution have given you a list of documents that you have reviewed, and you just said that you would have no objection for -- to a third of those documents to be admitted. So it would be useful for the Chamber if, after the break, you tell the Chamber which documents you are -- for which documents you have an objection to their admission, because there may well be a large number of documents that will raise no problem. However, it is for you to tell us, because I'm unable to determine what your views are on these documents. It is for you to tell us. We had thought initially that you had objections to the admission of any document that is -- that would not have been submitted to a witness. Now you just modified this view slightly by saying that according to you, there were documents that could be admitted. So that's already a good step forward. Now, it would be useful for the Chamber if next time you tell us, "I have objections to the admission of this and that and the other documents." Now, we have spent almost an hour and a half on procedural issues --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, Mr. President, I didn't change my position, although there are certain elements that -- on the basis of which you drew that conclusion. It is the subject of discussion that is being changed. On Thursday, as far as I understood the Prosecutor, perhaps I misunderstood him, perhaps the interpretation wasn't the right one, he asked for the remaining documents from those three files which he didn't have time to use during the examination, and he wanted those documents admitted into evidence, and that's what I was objecting to. Now, over the weekend, I received a much more extensive list, and many of these documents I'm not going to challenge. And if they are excerpts from my books, of course, I am not going to challenge them at all. I don't know about the translation, but that's the Court's problem. So I can state my views on that, but there are certain other documents from my book that are not excerpts from my books which the Prosecutor did not use and did not present to this witness during his examination. Well, let him wait for some other witness and present those documents to this other witness. You saw documents without signature, without dates, without any official type of marking, and had I not intervened straight away, maybe that would have been admitted into evidence too; it would have passed you by. You see that danger always exists and that is why I'm very cautious, perhaps I am abundantly cautious or exceedingly cautious, but what can I do? I can't change that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. The hearing is resumed. Mr. Seselj, you have the floor for the cross-examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, we have established, or rather we established on Thursday that the eight years that you've been working in the OTP of The Hague Tribunal, you participated in almost all the forms of activity of the OTP, which means that you participated in interviewing witnesses, interviewing suspects, preparing indictments, witness proofing for the Prosecution, and other kinds of work; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I don't believe that the witness's evidence was that he participated in preparing indictments. His testimony was that he provided input on -- when requested, he provided input to the lawyers who prepared the indictments.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not say that Mr. Theunens participated in writing indictments, but in preparing indictments. He was a consultant, an adviser. It's hardly possible for two people to write something together, but he did participate, and that is beyond doubt from his statement on Thursday.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Isn't that so, Mr. Theunens? He was an adviser for military matters.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would first like to answer the initial question where reference was made to eight years. As I stated initially, I started to work for the OTP on the 28th of June, 2001, so we are barely at seven years at this stage. To answer the second part of the question, it is correct that I work as a military intelligence analyst in the Office of the Prosecutor, that I'm requested by senior trial attorneys, trial attorneys, legal officers, investigators, to assist them with military matters, but it's impossible for me to determine to what extent the input or the information I provide to the people I mentioned is included in indictments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, do you, as the accused suggests, take part in the interviewing of witnesses, the proofing of the witnesses, and the other things that he mentioned, all the forms of activity of the OTP, that you prepare the indictments and all of this? Could you be more specific as to the exact role you play in relation to this indictment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see two parts in your question. I have participated in interviews of senior military witnesses and suspects, where I was there mainly to assist the people conducting the interview with military matters. When it concerned interviews of witnesses, so senior military witnesses, I sometimes also asked questions or I selected documents that could be shown to these witnesses during the interview, at the discretion of the person in charge of the interview. In relation to this particular indictment, I was sent, during the various stages of the preparation of the indictment, draft versions of the indictment where I only looked at the factual sections, where, for example, certain dates or certain events were discussed, or the names of structures or of people, and where then my input was sought in order to determine whether the information that was included in the draft indictment was correct. It is obvious, as I'm not a lawyer and have not had significant legal training, that I never got involved in legal matters, so I was never consulted and I never interfered or intermingled in the determination of legal issues, like counts and stuff like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But with respect to General Panic, were you one of those who questioned him or interviewed him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours, and I'm actually -- I'm pleased that I can provide maybe a more accurate picture of the interview, or at least one session of the interview, than what was said earlier in this courtroom. In my recollection, there were two sessions of meetings with General Zivota Panic. I only --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If Mr. Panic -- if Mr. Seselj wants to put questions to you about this, he'll do so, but of course what you understand, that I want to assess how close you are to the OTP. Vukovar is part of this case, and I'd like to know whether you interviewed or whether you took part in proofing sessions for Radic, Mrksic and Sljivancanin, whether you took part in the proofing of these three during the preparation of that particular trial, the Vukovar trial.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I participated in a number of proofing sessions for the Vukovar trial, specifically for a number of proofing sessions of senior military witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You confirmed here, Mr. Theunens, that you participated in witness proofing in various cases also, did you not? Do I remember correctly?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, but, I mean, I don't see a direct problem with that, unless I would start to do the job of what the lawyers are doing. My task, as a military intelligence analyst, only assists in -- only consists, excuse me, of assisting the lawyers who are actually doing the proofing, with legal matters. I also assist them with the selection of documents they could be -- that could be used during the proofing or in the court session, but that is -- that is all I do. I don't get involved in legal matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I never accused you of dealing in legal matters, but you answered all my questions on Thursday in the affirmative, that you participated in drawing up my indictment, that you participated in drawing up the amended, extended indictment, that you participated in proofing Prosecution witnesses, that you participated in suspect interviews, that you carry out proofing of witnesses, of course, together with others from the OTP within the scope of your expertise. I'm not challenging that. I'm not accusing you of being a legal expert at any point. And that you also signed a declaration that you would keep the secrets of the OTP. So I am drawing the conclusion here that you are a witness in your own case, as if Mr. Mundis were to testify here or Mr. Marcussen, or Madam Christina Dahl. You're all members of the OTP team, but you have different roles within that team; am I correct, Mr. Theunens?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think that is a misrepresentation of my role. I would like to bring us back to my report, because my report is actually the reason why I'm here, and I'd like to draw your attention to the fact that any claim that is made in this report is based on a document, and the document, the nature of the document, can be found in the footnotes. There is not one claim made in that report, or conclusion drawn in my report, which is not substantiated by one or more documents. Now, it is obviously up to the Honourable Judges and the Trial Chamber to determine the weight of my evidence, i.e., to determine the importance and the weight of the documents that have been included in my report. I also stated last week, and I wish to repeat it, that whether I wrote this report for the OTP or for some -- or in the Belgian military, or for a research institute, or for anybody else, it would have been the same report, because the contents of the report is determined by the sources I consulted. It is true that I consulted mainly documents that are available to the OTP, but as we discussed this morning, there is an extensive amount of what is called Rule 68 or exonerating material available to the OTP. So I think it would be incorrect to reduce my testimony and my report to just the fact that I am here as a representative who seems to be -- of the OTP who is testifying in his own trial, because I think that's inaccurate and incorrect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, these are preliminary matters. We are not dealing with the substance of your testimony or of your reports. These are preliminary questions we are putting to you, because we have to determine whether this so-called proximity with the OTP -- between you and the OTP may have led you to reach certain conclusions, rather than others. Therefore, it's a question that comes before what you've just explained.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honours, but I wanted to clarify my point of view from the start of the discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In the hypothetical situation, Mr. Theunens, in which Mr. Mundis or Mr. Marcussen were to appear as OTP experts, sitting in the chair you're sitting at now, they would of course not be testifying about military matters as experts; they would be testifying primarily to legal matters. But what would be the difference, in principle, between their expert testimony and your expert testimony, the difference in principle? Let's lay aside for the moment the fact that you are a military expert and they are, allegedly, legal experts. What would be the difference, in principle, between your appearance in the courtroom and theirs?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I cannot -- I don't know what Mr. Mundis or Mr. Marcussen would say or if they would compile a report, what this report would be about. But if they would do so and I would be competent in the matter they would address in their report, in their testimony, I would obviously look at it with a critical sense, as I as an analyst always do when doing my job, and then I would listen to what they say and then see whether there is any bias or not. Bias, as such, is an issue that -- or a problem that exists with intelligence analysts everywhere, and it's important to avoid any bias. And, first of all, discovering bias and avoiding it is one of the first things I learned doing my job, not only while doing my job but also during the training courses I attended in the course of my career. There are different forms of bias. Obviously, the fact that somebody works for a particular organisation can result in bias, but then it's up to that individual, in this situation myself, to avoid that the fact that one belongs to a particular organisation has an impact on the way how I do my job as an intelligence analyst; i.e., how to avoid that bias which would obviously be very -- would be a problem that could arise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, please listen to my questions carefully, and if possible, answer only what I'm asking you about. Don't give me responses to questions I didn't put. Don't extend the topic of this conversation too far, because as you know, I have little time at my disposal. I have no knowledge that Mr. Mundis or Mr. Marcussen participated in writing the indictment against me or that they participated in extending the indictment against me, or that they participated in interviewing Prosecution witnesses --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. We have a problem. There's a technical problem. We need to take a break. We'll just wait here for a few minutes. Fine. Things are working again now. Mr. Seselj, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, for example, Mr. Theunens, I have not a single piece of information showing that Mr. Mundis or Mr. Marcussen participated in drafting the indictment against me or in extending that indictment, or that they participated in interviewing potential witnesses and other preparations for this trial. I do have evidence, however, that you participated in drafting the indictment against me, drafting the extended indictment, interviewing witnesses, proofing witnesses, interviewing suspects, and so on and so forth. Am I correct in saying that I have more reason to believe in the impartiality of Mr. Mundis and Mr. Marcussen than I have to believe in yours? But please answer me briefly. The best would be to say "yes" or "no."

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, then my answer is, "No."

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, you are interested in the success of the indictment against me because you participated in its creation, you participated in preparing the trial, collecting documents, preparing and proofing witnesses and so on; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, my interest is -- and I've said the same, actually, to -- in the Vukovar trial when I was questioned there by the Defence attorney of Mr. Mrksic, that my interest is to provide, how small it can be, a contribution to justice, and if justice means -- I mean, just to rephrase, whatever this means for the indictment, that we'll know that at the end of the trial, but the most important and the driving factor in my work, and also the reason -- the main reason for me to come to the -- come and work for the OTP is to have justice prevail.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You know, Mr. Theunens, as you worked for years for the Belgian Intelligence Service, to what extent espionage, as an activity, is impartial. We were able to see this in the case of spies of the French Intelligence Service, Yves Tomic. Now we have a spy of the Belgian Intelligence Service; that's you. You both claim to be impartial. But I also believe that spies are partial, because I know what that service entails. So please don't try to justify yourself and claim that you're impartial. Everybody in the world knows to what extent spies are impartial. You completed a military academy of the Belgian Army --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, I have to interrupt you, because at line 9 of page 49 of the transcript, Mr. Seselj says that you're a spy, that you work for the Belgian Secret Services. What is the answer to this, "yes," "no"; do you have anything to say about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think Mr. Seselj has a wrong understanding of the concept of espionage, because espionage, as I know it and as it is also determined in literature on the subject matter of intelligence, consists of a covert method which is used by hostile intelligence services to acquire information dealing with national security of a country to which they are not entitled. I have never been involved in such activities.
