As far as Mr. Tomic is concerned, I have not read his CV, but listening to parts of his testimony, I would be surprised if he had ever been involved in such activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, I know very well what espionage is, but let's take it step by step, and then we'll come to the merits of the issue of espionage and what you did in the Balkans as a NATO officer. We have to take it step by step. You completed the military academy of the Belgian Army; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was never in the Balkans as a NATO officer. I participated in two missions as a member of the United Nations Protection Forces and then as a member of the United Nations Transitional Administration for Eastern Slavonia. And my third assignment consisted of a national assignment where, as a member of the Belgian Armed Forces, I accomplished certain tasks in the SFOR headquarters. And indeed I completed the military academy at the Belgian Royal Military Academy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: As an officer of the United Nations, you sent intelligence reports to certain structures of the United Nations, but also to the Belgian Intelligence Service and the NATO headquarters; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have provided a CV which is part of the report or annex which establishes -- or which provides an overview of my professional activities, both during my time at ICTY as well as prior to my time at ICTY. For what my professional activities prior to June 2001 are concerned, I am subject to the Belgian law on security clearances and classification from 11 December 1998 which prohibits me from discussing detailed matters with persons who have no need to know or who have no Belgian security clearance. Even my tasks as a platoon commander in the Belgian Armed Forces, when I was stationed in Germany, are the subject of this prohibition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Theunens. I've taken note of your answer. Mr. Seselj is asking you the following question: When you were an UNPROFOR member, did you ever send reports to the Belgian Secret Services and did you ever send reports to the NATO Intelligence Services? The question was very clear and straightforward. In answer to this question, you tell us that because of your particular status, you are prohibited from answering. Have I got it correctly, did I understand correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, Your Honours. I can discuss the matters to the extent that they are covered in the written CV that is part of my report, but I cannot talk about relations between the service I worked in and other services, the focus of intelligence efforts, methods that were applied, sources, and other classified matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I just wanted to underline that the witness is in the situation that Your Honours surely would have had with all witnesses of this nature, military staff and police staff who are subject to these kind of restrictions in their domestic jurisdictions, and I think what we have here is a situation where the witness can talk about his tasks, but he cannot go into operational details for reasons that are obvious and well known to everyone in -- from domestic systems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, your avoidance of an answer, Mr. Theunens, is the best answer, in my view, because everything is clear now. And the Prosecutor needn't jump to his feet as if stung, because I have the right to prepare the witness for my next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marcussen, what did you want to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I object to the mis-qualification of this. The witness is not avoiding to answer the question. The witness is under an obligation not to discuss operational details, and it's not that the witness is not willing to answer the accused's questions when they are within the bounds of what he can speak to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. I understand, and I suppose my fellow Judges have understood as well, what it's all about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After considering the matter, we are rather puzzled about this. The question put to the witness was very straightforward. So, Witness, you can't confirm or deny anything; you're just telling us, "I can't answer because of my status as a Belgian military officer, and I have to abide by some rules," as such, although you're also an international civil servant? Do not forget that we are here within the framework of international justice.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honours, and I think maybe it's helpful that I make the clarification. Obviously, it is clear that when I was working in the UNPROFOR and UNPF and subsequently UNTAES headquarters, it is clear that I compiled what we call military information reports, assessments, other documents, for the members of the UN headquarters, as well as relevant authorities outside the UN headquarters, including sometimes providing elements of information that would be used for replies to questions from the Security Council. But for any relations I may have had or did not have with my -- the service I worked for in Belgium or a NATO organisation, that is subject matter -- that would be subject matter of the 11th of December, 1998 law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Yes, that's how we understood your answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One more thing. Within the UNPROFOR, were you allowed, because of the rules of engagement that prevailed at UNPROFOR, were you allowed to keep contacts with your original services in your own country?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's a very complicated matter. Why? Because UNPROFOR was sent as a peacekeeping mission, which means that there is a peace agreement and that the parties are willing to implement the agreement, and that they will do all efforts in order to continue with that implementation. Very soon, from the earliest stages of the deployment of UNPROFOR, it became clear that UNPROFOR was not a peacekeeping mission, because in simple terms there was no peace to keep. And then it became clear that the various troop-contributing nations who noticed that actually their soldiers were exposed to dangers which went beyond the dangers and the risks one would expect from a peacekeeping mission, that various countries undertook efforts in order to better protect their forces, including the collection and exchange of intelligence and information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, but Chapter 7 clearly shows that the objective is not only to maintain peace, but to establish it as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours. And, for example, UNTAES, the later mission, was indeed sent under Chapter 7. However -- and the UNCRO mandate, which replaced UNPROFOR in Bosnia and Herzegovina -- in Croatia, excuse me, also made references to Chapter 7 of the UN Charter. But the initial resolution that established UNPROFOR, in my recollection, makes reference to Chapter 6 of the UN Charter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. I see that although you stated that you are just a military man, you also have some knowledge in law, and that's always a good thing. Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'm surprised, Mr. Theunens, by the fact that you're now referring to the provisions of Belgian law which prohibits you from providing information about your activities. Now -- for many reasons. What am I interested -- what would I be interested in Belgian laws for? Belgium was an aggressive country in the war against the Serb people; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't think that is a correct representation of the facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well. But during your testimony in the trial against General Mrksic, Colonel Sljivancanin and Major Radic, when asked by one of the Defence counsel, you confirmed that as an officer of the United Nations, you provided intelligence information to the Belgian Army; and that confirmation of yours is to be found on page 10754 of the transcript in the Vukovar Troika trial. And I assume through e-court and your computers, you can have that up on your screen straight away, Judges. 10754 is the page number. Did you indeed confirm that, assert that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, that isn't -- I apologise for the transcript. That's an incomplete quotation of my answer. It's correct that the Defence attorney of Mr. Mrksic asked me whether, while I was working for UNPROFOR, I sent reports, and he said "reports," not specifically intelligence reports, to the Belgian Armed Forces. I first mentioned to the Judges that -- that there was a law on classification and security clearances. I may have not used the exact terminology, but -- or the same terminology, but I said that I was subject to legal limitations. And then the Presiding Judge, the Honourable Judge, Judge Parker, said that, "We understand this, but just answer 'yes' or 'no'." And then I said, "Yes."

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And, Mr. Theunens, since you said "yes" then, then from the Belgian espionage, they rubbed your nose in it, and now in these proceedings against me, in this trial, you don't want to state either yes or no; isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, who is a very intelligent man, is trying to make you say something which you don't want to say. This is why Mr. Marcussen is on his feet. Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Indeed, and I'm not even sure that it's not that the witness want to say this. The witness is not at liberty to discuss these matters, and he cannot answer these questions. So -- and the accused is well aware of this. And, frankly, I also question the relevance of this line of questioning to the issue of the witness's report and his work as an expert for the Office of the Prosecutor. So I think, first of all, it's an irrelevant line of questioning that the accused is pursuing, and he has been informed about the impossibility of the witness to address these questions, and I would like to request that the Chamber to direct him not to continue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, the witness specified that he could not answer these questions. He's a Belgian officer. He needs to abide by the bylaws or internal laws. We do not need to abide by these rules, but you cannot put these questions to him. So he says that he needs to abide by these rules, so please move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Interpretation] Mr. President, I hope that you're not going to count that in my time. Now, this witness took part, in 1995, as an officer of the United Nations, in preparing the Croatian Storm and Flash Operations against the Republic of Serbia and Krajina. At the time he had his headquarters in Zagreb, and he knew full well that these operations were being prepared, but did nothing to prevent them, to say the least. So he's directly involved in the conflict on the territory of the former Yugoslavia, because Croatia's aggression against Serbian Krajina was realised with direct assistance from NATO; and we have countless evidence to bear that out. And he took part in all that, and now he appears here as an unbiased, impartial witness, and I have to devote a whole hour to his role in those events as an officer of the Belgian armed forces. And he, in advance, states that he is not at liberty to disclose anything about his years of service working for the Belgian Intelligence Service. Well, what's the point of me cross-examining him at all, then?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, Mr. Seselj claims that in 1995, at the time you were a member of UNPROFOR, you purportedly prepared, together with the Croatians, the Storm and Flash Operations. So this is true, this is not true; what can you say about this? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, this is obviously not true. I worked as a military information officer in the UNPROFOR UNPF headquarters, and, I mean, if Mr. Seselj wants, we can go into the details of what exactly I did, and in relation to storm-and-flash. But I think it's a false claim and there's no fact whatsoever to support this kind of political claim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Seselj, he's answered the question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, in this belated curriculum vitae, because I was provided with two pages belatedly, under point 5, line 3, it says that from December 1994 until October 1995, this witness worked at UNPROFOR headquarters in Zagreb, and on the following affairs: Monitoring, analysis and evaluation of the political and military situation in Croatian, Bosnia-Herzegovina and the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia, as well as the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia on strategic operational and tactical levels. That's what he did. Now, I have documents to show that Croatia officially informed UNPROFOR forces that it was preparing an aggression and that it asked those forces to move out of the axes along which the Croatian Army would move during the aggression, which was done, because not a single United Nations soldier stood up to the aggression, provided resistance, or attempted to protect the civilian population, which was its mission. Now, as you're bringing me to the situation where the witness refuses to answer, I'll move on, I'll no longer insist on that, because as far as I'm concerned, that was the most convincing answer that the witness has yet given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's better to move on to another topic. But would you like to respond to this fact? This is Mr. Seselj's theory. He says that there was some degree of collusion between UNPROFOR and the Croatian Army. And according to Mr. Seselj, the best proof of this is that when the offensive was launched, UNPROFOR troops did not stand in the way. So either you say, "I've got nothing to say," "This is true," "This is not true." What do you have to say to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is obviously not true, in the sense that when you look at the size of these operations, they were planned and prepared months ahead. And it is only, I think as far as Operation Storm is concerned, one or two hours in advance that the Croatian authorities informed the senior command level of UNPF, that was General Janvier, the force commander, of the upcoming operation. However, as was clear to everyone at that stage who was following the situation in Croatia, we didn't have to wait for that phone call from the Croats to Janvier to know that the Croats were preparing a large-scale operation against the Krajina. And if you want and if Mr. Seselj wants, we can go into more detail about that. As I mentioned earlier, I can talk about my activities in the various peacekeeping headquarters, but I can't not address issues that deal directly with the activities of the Belgian service I belonged to prior and after my participation in these peacekeeping operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When you completed the military academy, you gained the title of second lieutenant, did you not?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the rank of second lieutenant is given in the third year of military academy, in the division I was in, the all-arms division.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So what rank did you have when you completed the military academy at the very end?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was still a second lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That's what I'm saying. As a second lieutenant, you left the military academy, having completed your training there. The highest command functions in the Belgian Army that you occupied was the commander of a tank platoon; right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was also the -- during the time period I was a platoon commander, I also was the acting company commander during several months.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Theunens, when I did my military service, compulsory military service as a rank-and-file soldier, I replaced the command of a captain, captain first class, in a third of the military training, because with a PhD. I did my military service, so he gave me the entire military education sector to deal with. You were never a company commander; you could have commanded a company by taking over if somebody -- the commander went to the toilet or something or was engaged elsewhere, so give me precise answers. I have a document saying that you were named platoon commander. Right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not clear to me, what the question is, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The highest command post that you occupied in the units of the Belgian Army was platoon commander, a commander of a tank platoon; right? Am I right there?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, that is not correct, because as I have explained, during several months I replaced my company commander while he was attending language courses.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: While he was attending languages courses. He might have been on leave, for example, too, gone off on a holiday. Very well, Mr. Theunens. But even if you were a company commander, it is too low a commanding rank for you to be able to be called an expert on any matter; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think that's a question the honourable Judges will deal with.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What, in your opinion, Mr. Theunens, does the word "expert" mean and denote?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't think my opinion has any relevance in that context. There are articles in the ICTY Statute that determine the requirements that apply to whether somebody can be called an expert or not, and it's up to the honourable Judges to decide whether the person who is proposed by one of the parties to testify or to file a report and/or testify as an expert merits that title, yes or no, and then also to decide about the ultimate issue, i.e., what the weight of the evidence of that person will be.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, I am testing your credibility. You must answer my question. What, in your opinion, does a specific concept mean? And in this case, the concept of expert. You can say you don't know how to answer that, but you can't get away from it by giving broader explanations. The word "expert" in every language on this planet of ours has a specific meaning, it means the same. So what, in your opinion, does the word "expert" mean? And I'm testing your professionalism, whether you know what the term "expert" means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: We have had with other witnesses the same kind of exercise, of getting into semantics and the witness's knowledge of specific terms. Whether or not the witness can give a different definition of "expert" that the accused is happy with is utterly irrelevant to any issue before the Chamber, and I think we should just move on to something that is relevant. That would be my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that would be better. It would be better to move on to another topic. You said, in any case, that it would be for the Judges to assess whether you are an expert or not at the end of the day, but let me remind you that a decision was handed out on the matter and the question will focus on whether, yes or no, your expert report should be admitted. But as far as you are concerned, Witness, what is an expert in your eyes? An automotive expert, a plumbing expert, a ballistics expert. What makes an expert specific, what is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In general terms, Your Honour, I would say an expert, and you've given a number of examples, is somebody who, by his or her training, education, and professional or other relevant activities, has acquired knowledge which goes beyond the level of the average citizen in a particular subject matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Am I right, Mr. Theunens, in saying the following: That an expert is a person who has the most knowledge and greatest experience in a certain field? Would my definition of "expert" be more complete and better than the one you've just improvised?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I did not improvise. And, secondly, well, it's Mr. Seselj's definition. I may have another definition. If we go out on the streets in The Hague and we ask four people for their definition, we may -- we have four different versions. I think we're turning in circles, I gave the initial answer where I stated that it's up to the honourable Judges to decide about that. That would also be my final answer to this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, once again it would be better to move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am going to move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, did you gain the title of "Master of Science," Mr. Theunens?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. When I finalized my education at the military academy, it was still called "Licentiaat" in Dutch, or "License" in French, and I understand with the various measures in the European level to equalise university degrees, that the License of the military academy corresponds with the Master's.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So you gained the rank of Master of Science on the basis of the application of the so-called Bologna declaration; is that right, Mr. Theunens?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I gained it because of the studies I completed successfully, and what happened afterwards is beyond my control.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'm not accusing you of applying the Bologna declaration. Don't misunderstand me. The Bologna declaration has put pay to all of European education. But I'm just asking you -- I'm just saying the Bologna declaration was applied, and it was on the basis of that declaration that you gained the rank that corresponds to the title or rank of Master of Science. Just say whether I'm right there or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Bologna, you're talking about the town in Italy, not Boulogne in France. When I look at the transcript, it has Boulogne, but I believe this is Bologna in Italy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Could you answer that question briefly, please?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: To keep it short, the answer is, "Yes."

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, before it was applied, the Bologna declaration was applied in Belgium, and I'm saying the word correctly, Bologna, you prepared a Master's thesis on the subject of international politics; right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not entirely correct, Your Honours. While I was working in Brussels, I attended an evening course which would, if you complete the education or the studies, would allow you to use the title of Master's of International Politics, but that was not an official title. Now, before I could complete the studies, I was asked or invited to come and work for the Office of the Prosecutor, so I never finalised the studies and I didn't complete a thesis. I had hoped to do so, but my professional activities in The Hague prevented me from doing so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Theunens. All I wanted was a brief answer, but you've answered my question affirmatively. You were prevented from becoming an MA, but in the meantime you gained that rank thanks to the Bologna declaration, and we've dealt with that matter. Now let's move on to another area, another question. I'm going to tell you what this is like in Serbia or what it was like in the former Yugoslavia, and tell me whether that corresponds to the situation in Belgium, in what I'm going to present now. In Serbia, in the former Yugoslavia, an officer, having completed the military academy, could advance regularly up to the rank of captain first class, which corresponds to your rank of commander. Now, after that, that person would have to proceed or not proceed to the Command Staff Academy, which lasts for two years, and then take an examination for major. And if he passed, then he would be a major, and then lieutenant colonel and then colonel. He could move up the ranks. And then after that, some people, not everyone, had the possibility of attending war school, or the School of National Defence, as it was called, which also lasts for two years, and a general's thesis and general's examination is then passed, and Doctor of Science is the rank achieved after the general's examination. So the MA would correspond to a Major and the general's examination would give you the title of a PhD. Is that how it is in Belgium, does it correspond to the situation in Belgium?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not, Your Honours, because the training courses that are attended after the military academy, i.e., we have a one-year senior officer candidate staff course, excuse me, which I attended, there is later on a one-year -- what we call a third cycle, but that is a senior officers' course. Those courses do not provide any academic title, even though one attends additional education and a thesis needs to be written or other tests and exams passed. They do not provide an academic title.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: First of all, in Serbia you don't get an academic title, either, but the major's examination is of the same rank as a Master of Science or Master of Arts. A major cannot say that he is a Master of Science. The general's examination is equivalent to a PhD examination, although a general will never claim to be a PhD. But I'm speaking of the level of the rank of the examination. For example, when a colonel completes war school and passes a general's examination, he is not automatically promoted to the rank of general. This depends on other circumstances; the number of generals' posts that are vacant and so on and so forth. But once he becomes a major general, he has the same rank as an assistant professor and so on and so forth. Am I correct, Mr. Theunens? But please respond as briefly as you can. If I'm wrong, just say, "No," and we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this may be the situation in Serbia, but it doesn't apply to the Belgian Armed Forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He would like to know whether things work the same way. In Belgium, you can be a lieutenant and have a university degree and be a PhD holder. Can you confirm this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. This is not -- the only thing that is established is that somebody who attends military academy and concludes his studies successfully, he will be, nowadays, a Master or an engineer. And what happens later on, well, there can be people who acquire PhD two years later but it has no relevance for their rank or not, unless there is a special recruitment for experts in a particular subject matter, like legal affairs, where the fact that they obtained an additional degree, I mean, academic title, can accelerate their career.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, you may have misunderstood my question. I don't know what the interpretation was. I was a PhD, but in the army I had a very low rank. A PhD does not entail a high military rank automatically. But had I wanted to gain employment in the army with a PhD, I would have been a military employee with the same rank as a colonel. I never acquired that rank because I was never employed in the military. But a colonel with a war school has the same rank as a PhD. But evidently the witness doesn't understand this, so we will move on. Mr. Theunens --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, I think the witness has understood and the Bench has also understood. In the Belgian Army, there is no equivalence between the ranks and the degrees. You can be an officer in the Belgian Army without holding or having a PhD. And you can be a lieutenant in the Belgian Army and still have a PhD.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's not the essence of what I'm insisting on, but I won't waste time. I'm speaking of the level, not on gaining certain rights based on an academic title, but of the equivalence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Witness, would you, with your qualifications and rank of Komandant or Captain First Class be able to be an expert on anything in Belgium?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, with the rank of lieutenant, as you can see from my written CV, I was designated to provide the briefings to the chief of defence staff and other senior officials on matters relating to the situation in the Balkans. So just to clarify that, there is no direct equivalent or direct link between rank and knowledge, especially not in the armed forces I functioned in.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, in the course of your examination-in-chief, you explained to us the methodology used in intelligence work, and you expounded this in certain points. There's no point in repeating this. But have you ever dealt with scholarly or scientific methodology?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, during -- I will provide two elements of information to this question. First of all, during my education at the military academy, one of the first courses we had was a course in the consulting of sources as well as source critique, and it started on a very mundane level on how to visit a library, but obviously became more complicated. The second element I would like to mention is that during the time period I worked as an intelligence analyst, I've been in touch with obviously people from various environments, including university professors or people working on a PhD and so on, and we would discuss methodology they applied, as well as what we applied, and we came to the conclusion that there was a lot of similarity between, on one hand, the intelligence cycle and, on the other hand, the scientific methodology applied by -- for example, by PhD candidates or university professors.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'm drawing the conclusion from your response that you did not delve into the methodology, but that you came across people who did. This reminds me of my Aunt Mira, who never even completed primary school, but she has an understanding of medicine because she had a doctor in her neighbourhood. I'm asking you about scientific and scholarly methodology, and you are speaking of methods.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, we are very happy to know that you have an Aunt Mira who was well versed in medicine without being a doctor, but he said that the methodology used in the intelligence services was very similar to the methodology used in other areas, like university professors. This is what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, did you ever work on a project, a scientific or expert project, in the military field before you became an employee of the International Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's not clear to me what Mr. Seselj means by "scientific or expert project."

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, that's the whole problem, that you don't understand this. Anyone engaged in scholarship or science and who is an expert in a field knows what a scholarly project or an expert project is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, do you believe that only university professors can be experts? I find that a little bit strange. I am, myself, a professor, so I believe I know what we do and what we don't do. Nonetheless, you can be an expert even if you don't have any scientific knowledge or if you don't use any kind of scientific methodology. You can still be an expert. Why not? Whatever the case may be, I believe it is for the Judges to settle the matter, and it's not for you to comment on the answers provided by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, I agree with what my fellow Judge has just said. You can be an expert without automatically holding a title or without being a professor at university. For example, take the case in the automotive industry, you're going to ask somebody to talk about a spark plug. In the automotive industry, perhaps a mechanic can also provide an expert opinion on how a spark plug works in an engine of a car, so you don't have to -- like you, you don't have to have the title of university professor to claim that you are an expert. Maybe this is what is making our life difficult.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm convinced, Mr. President and Madame Judge, that there is no university professor who could fix your car as a good mechanic can, but what we have before us is an expert report on more than 400 pages, which should have been done according to scientific methodology. It's not the same thing as fixing a car. An expert has to have the best knowledge of a certain field. He has to be among those who are most familiar with a certain field. And for an expert report of this kind, he also has to be conversant with scientific methodology. You can say that I'm wrong in your judgement, which you will eventually hand down, but what I'm trying to show you now is that this man cannot be an expert of any kind. You can say later on that I'm wrong --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, please show in what way this gentleman's expert report did not apply any scientific method. In what way does his report contain failings? What should he have done, what didn't he do, as far as you're concerned? And you will be able to highlight this by putting your question properly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I fully agree with you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, what scientific method did you use in compiling this expert report? Identify your scientific method.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, as was explained through the examination, the method I applied was the method I am familiar with called "the intelligence cycle." I can explain again the various steps and phase of the intelligence cycle. And I realized, when doing research on various aspects of the intelligence cycle, that this kind of methodology is also applied by certain universities. And as I explained earlier, when I gave an earlier answer to the question, it was quite similar to the methodology applied by people I was in contact with while I was still working in the armed forces, for example, PhD students or professors who were also dealing with matters related to the Balkans.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So, Mr. Theunens, you do not understand the difference between methodology, as a science, and methodics, as an expert discipline, and your method of the intelligence cycle, which belongs within the domain of intelligence methodics, you are trying to represent it here as a scientific methodology. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, my understanding was that I was asked which methodology I applied when compiling the report, and I replied that I used the intelligence cycle when compiling the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Your intelligence cycle belongs in the methodics of your intelligence work, prescribed by your intelligence service. It has nothing to do with scientific methodology. Do you know, Mr. Theunens, what epistemology is?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You don't know. It's a theory of scientific knowledge. It examines logical foundations, of provisions, of the possibility of scientific knowledge, and so on and so forth, and methodology is based on epistemology. I'm asking you this question, because I observed that in your expert report you confused ontological, gnosiological and axiological aspects of the problem, so I have to ask you whether you know what ontology is?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Theunens, what gnosiology is?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know what axiology is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you are submitting Mr. Theunens to an exam right now. However, there was something that was interesting in your initial questions, which was determining whether the methodology used in military intelligence can be applied in the field of work that was entrusted to him by the OTP; in other words, relationships between the volunteers and the events on the ground, et cetera. This may be relevant, but now if you submit the witness to an exam about ontology, gnosiology, et cetera, he will answer that he does not know, because I think you should not forget that he is basically a military officer. He is not a university professor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, what I'm asking him about is secondary school-level knowledge. Every secondary school pupil in Serbia, and I assume in France, knows that ontology is the theory of your existence, gnosiology is the theory of knowledge and axiology the theory of values. He says doesn't know this, and now you keep insisting on saying he's an expert. I'm trying to show you that he's an ignoramus. The OTP has represented him as an expert, and you're trying to prevent my expert questions. I have already disqualified him as any kind of expert. You can declare him to be whatever you like. What can I do about it? But he lacks even secondary school knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, as you don't know these things, I'm powerless to put expert questions to you, questions of scientific methodology. I can, however, put specific questions to you, concrete questions. How could you write, in this report of yours, that -- it's on page 3 of your report, page 3 in the Serbian -- that the Yugoslav People's Army consisted of the General Staff and three branches of service, ground forces, air force and air defence, and navy? How could you write that, as a military expert, the top expert?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I included this paragraph in the executive summary, and it's a summary of the information that is included elsewhere in the report, including there the legal references on which this summarising sentence was based. It is correct that there is no legal reference that states that the General Staff was part of the JNA, but I thought it would assist the reader just to summarise the various legal references and come to this conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you, Mr. Theunens, consider that this report would be read by a fool who knows nothing, and then you could comfortably say that the JNA is comprised of the General Staff and three branches of service? What did you think? How could you introduce the General Staff as an integral part of the JNA? Where is your legal basis for that? On what basis did you do that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: The second part of the question -- I think the first part of this question, implying that he -- that the expert thinks the Court is a fool and things like that, is inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, I didn't call the expert a fool. I really don't know what sort of interpretation you're getting. I said, "Did you consider that this report would be read by some fool with no understanding of this so that you could pass on to him this information that the army was -- consisted of the General Staff and three branches?" I can call the expert an ignoramus, I can say that he's lying about certain things, but why on earth would I call him a fool? I'm a person with gentlemanly manners, I'm a Chetnik Vojvoda, so why would I call him a fool? Don't laugh, Mr. Marcussen, because it's contagious.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will attempt to answer the first part of the question. On page 19 in the English part of the report, in the English version of the report, the first part, I have a title "The General Staff of the SFRY Armed Forces," and there it is stated that the SFRY General Staff is in the composition of the Federal Secretariat for People's Defence and carries out staff and other expert jobs. The reference I use for that is 65 ter number 496, the SFRY Presidency order number 26 dated the 13th of August, 1987. It is this Presidency order which transforms the General Staff of the JNA to the General Staff of the SFRY Armed Forces, which is further explained in the section on the Jadinstvo [phoen] reorganisation plan which you can find in page 26, English page 26, of Part 1 of the report. And through the Jadinstvo, the General Staff of the JNA becomes the General Staff of the SFRY Armed Forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I have to observe, then, that you had at your disposal a document from 1987, where the General Staff of the JNA was transformed into the General Staff of the Armed Forces, and in spite of this, in the introductory part of your expert report and in the executive summary which I received a few days ago, you state that the JNA was composed of a general staff and three branches. How was this possible, then? Was this written by different people, one wrote one thing and the other wrote the other? Doesn't this look like a schizophrenic expert report? In one place, you say one thing, and in another place, you say another, like a split personality. Or was this written by more than one person and you didn't check what the other one wrote? What's true, Mr. Theunens?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the report was compiled by myself and nobody else, and it is true that at first glance there is this difference between what I state in the executive summary or the summarising paragraph, on the one hand, and in the body of the report, on the other hand, but my understanding of the General Staff was that even when it was renamed and repositioned from "General Staff of the JNA" into "General Staff of the SFRY Armed Forces," that this had no significant impact on its structure, of its role, except of course that its competencies as General Staff of the SFRY Armed Forces became wider because it also encompassed the TO. So if Mr. Seselj wants to make a big thing of that, that is his choice, but I hope that my explanations can clarify the matter for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, I'm not making an issue of that, but the General Staff of the Armed Forces, the JNA and the Territorial Defence were both subordinated to it in their entirety; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, but it's not that they are all subordinate to the General -- yeah, that is correct. I mean, when the General Staff of the JNA became the General Staff of the SFRY Armed Forces, it became the authority over the JNA and the TO, whereby I wish to clarify that the General Staff or the chief of the General Staff, as such, has no command role. He can only forward the orders issued by the Federal Secretary for People's Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In the structure of command of the Armed Forces, the presidency of the SFRY is at the top, then the Secretariat for National Defence, then the General Staff of the Armed Forces; isn't that correct? Am I right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And the General Staff, as the third level here, is in charge both of the JNA and the Territorial Defence equally; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, after 1987 [Realtime transcript read in error "1997"], that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Why, then, did you write that the General Staff was part of the JNA when the General Staff was above the JNA? That's my basic question. Why is this in your report?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, I'm slightly lost right now, because 1997 was mentioned and the years following 1997, but we are interested in 1991, 1992, 1993, 1994. 1997 has no interest for the Judges. What is important is the chain of command. Who makes the decisions at the top and how the order is forwarded within the period of 1991, 1992, 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm talking about 1987, not 1997. From 1987 onwards, that's what I'm insisting on. So there's no misunderstanding, perhaps the problem was in the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. So starting in 1987, what is the chain of command, according to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, starting from the top level, i.e., the political level, we go from the Supreme Command, consisting of the SFRY Presidency, which is led by the president of the SFRY Presidency, through the staff of the Supreme Command, which consists of the Federal Secretary for People's Defence, assisted by his Secretariat, as well as the chief of the General Staff, assisted by his General Staff, downwards to the operational units. In clear terms, it means that the Federal Secretary for People's Defence could issue orders directly to the military districts, so he doesn't have to go through the Chief of General Staff, even though there are examples of orders transiting from the Federal Secretary for People's Defence through the chief of the General Staff to the operational units, and at the operational level, the highest level in peacetime would be the military district level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. So here we're dealing with a very significant issue. Correct me if I'm wrong, please. The Supreme Command is composed of the Presidency with the president, and assisted by the staff of the Presidency in which the Secretariat to the Defence plays a particular role, and the Defence Secretariat forwards orders to the units without having to go through the head of the Main Staff; is that it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours, and that is different from what exists in certain Western countries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Now, in order to account for Mr. Seselj's concerns, the JNA and the Territorial Defence, the TO, are at a lower level. They receive orders from the Defence Secretariat; is that it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, but the difference -- or the change that is made in 1987 is that the Chief of General Staff, when he receives orders from the Federal Secretary for People's Defence, he can forward them directly to JNA and TO, whereas before there would be a direct line from the Federal Secretary of People's Defence to the TO, without passing through the Chief of General Staff, because before 1987 he would only be responsible for the JNA. After 1987, the chief would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if there's one thing we should keep in mind, it's that starting in 1987, the orders forwarded to the TO go through the head of the General Staff, which was not the case before.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours, and also the TO becomes subordinated to the -- what is called the strategic operational level units, i.e., the military districts, whereas before they were on a parallel level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, please carry on, but these things had to be clarified because unless they were clarified, we were in danger of being totally at a loss. But the time of break has come, so 20 minutes' break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. We'll stop at a quarter past 1.00. Mr. Seselj, you've used up one hour and 17 minutes so far. Let me also remind everyone that tomorrow, we'll be starting at 9.00 and not at 8.30 a.m., because my fellow Judges won't be sitting in the Delic case tomorrow afternoon, and we'll be sitting from 9.00 a.m. tomorrow. On the other hand, on Thursday, we'll start at 8.30, and we'll sit until a quarter past 1.00 on Thursday. I would also like to notify you of the fact that tomorrow Judge Lattanzi won't be with us, for professional reasons. That's tomorrow and the day after tomorrow. Judge Harhoff and myself will be here, of course. This by way of an introduction, and now let me give the floor to Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, you should know that Yugoslavia, somewhere towards the end of the 1960s, developed a specific concept of the doctrine and system of the All People's Defence; right? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of that, Your Honours, and that is discussed in my report on -- in the English version on page 4, where I mention that the doctrine of All People's Defence was published as the official military doctrine in 1969.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Would you be able, Mr. Theunens, to tell us, just in a few words, what the substance of the concept of All People's Defence is? In a few words, how would you explain the concept of All People's Defence to somebody who doesn't know anything about it?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, it would mean that all human and materiel resources are being used in order to defend the country. And, for example, I make reference to a legal manual for commanding officers dating from 1976 in my report, when I first explain what "All People's Defence" means.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you agree that the essence of the concept of All People's Defence is the Marxist concept of an armed peoples?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have not studied All People's Defence from that angle, i.e., from the Marxist angle, to see whether there is any similarity with the Marxist concept of defence, so I would not be able to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, you could have found that in the numerous literature in which explanations are given for the concept of All People's Defence, you needn't read all of Marx and Engels. You could have learned it from the literature, and there is a lot of literature on this subject. You could have come by that elementary information. Now, how would you, in a few words, define the doctrine of All People's Defence? All People's Defence, yes.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think I answered that question. The doctrine consists of using all resources that are available, both on the human as well as on the materiel level, for defensive purposes, i.e., to struggle against an aggressor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, you said that a moment ago, when I asked you what the concept of it was. So the concept and doctrine can't be the same thing. You're repeating what you said about doctrine, so that means you don't know what "concept" means and what "doctrine" means. Now, if I tell you that doctrine -- the doctrine of All People's Defence is a doctrine of waging an all people's war or defence, or defensive war, would you agree that is the substance of what it means when we say "doctrine"?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, my understanding of the word "doctrine" is that "doctrine" means -- I mean military doctrine are the guiding principles used by armed forces in order to implement political goals. I think that when Mr. Seselj provided the answer to his own question, he said twice the same, but that's maybe a translation issue.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that context you're dealing with at the moment, Witness, were we talking about defence against an external aggressor or against an enemy coming from the country itself, from inside the country?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the focus is on an external aggressor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj is asking you to define this doctrine, and the word "national" has been used, "war of national defence." And let me follow up on the question put to you by my fellow Judge. If the nation is threatened from within, can this doctrine be applied then as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The doctrine emphasizes the importance of the fact that it includes all nations and nationalities of the socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, whereby the JNA would be a federal armed force, i.e., which covers all the republics of the SFRY and which represents all the republics, and the TO would be established and organised and so on by the republic. Now, as I replied to the question of Judge Lattanzi, the documents I have reviewed, for example, the military manuals, all focus on external threats. However, there are, within the SFRY armed forces, organs like, for example, the Security Administration, UB, who deal specifically with threats, foreign as well as internal threats against the armed forces. Also, on the federal Minister of the Interior level, there would be organs or services that deal with threats from inside against the stability and the order within the SFRY. And as I said, the focus of the doctrine and the military -- the use of the armed forces is all focused on an external threat, whereby an external force invades the country. There was talk at the time of a plan S-1 and later plan S-2, depending on whether the threat came from the Warsaw Pact and then that was reviewed into a threat coming from NATO countries, and this was then the main guidance or guiding plan for the armed forces in order to establish defensive plans. So external threats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The national issue may be on the agenda. Before Vukovar, the national issue involves everyone, Muslims, Croats, everyone. I'm talking of the use of this national -- word "national." But if nationalistic tendencies appear within one of these components, can the authorities intervene to guarantee this national concept within the Yugoslav meaning of the term? My question may be rather complex, but you might be able to answer it nevertheless.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours, and that's exactly what we -- what we see when we see -- when we look at the developments in early 1991, that is, that the Federal Secretary for People's Defence, Kadijevic, considers that the Presidency, his Supreme Commander should actually give him instructions in order to act against cessionist forces, including in Slovenia and later Croatia. For example, during the Presidency sessions in January 1991 and March 1991, Kadijevic asks the Supreme Command, i.e., the members of the Presidency, to decree a state of emergency which would create the legal conditions for the SFRY armed forces or what remains of the SFRY armed forces to act against the internal threat. But when I was answering the question first, I was focusing on what I saw in the military manuals. The military manuals, as far as I've seen them, do not discuss fighting against an internal enemy, except for the specific manuals for the Security Administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Theunens, what the difference is between the concept and doctrine? I see that you mix up those two concepts.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know the difference between "concept" and "doctrine," Your Honours, but when Mr. Seselj asked the question about "concept," I refer to my report, where I use the word "doctrine" to explain what All People's Defence was all about.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, that's where the problem lies, Mr. Theunens, because you're mixing up the notion of "concept" and "doctrine." You give the same answers when I ask you about what "concept" means and what "doctrine" means, and neither answer is satisfactory and based on fact. But here's a new question for you: In what case would it be against an internal enemy, based on the legal system of Yugoslavia, would the use of the armed forces be allowed? Just in brief terms, in what situation?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is the question about a legal reference or do you want me to explain what the Supreme Command, i.e., the Presidency could do and how this mechanism would be implemented?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You are allegedly the expert, Mr. Theunens. I'm not interested in what the Presidency could do as the Supreme Command. What I'm interested in is a brief answer to my question. Since you've already stated that the armed forces are primarily oriented towards standing up to a potential aggressor or external enemy, then in what case would the armed forces be permitted to resist an internal enemy? Just give me a brief answer in two or three words, if you know the answer. If not, we can move on.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if -- if -- the military does what the Supreme Command, i.e., the Presidency, tells it to do. Now, legally we know from the Constitution, Article 240 [Realtime transcript read in error "214"], that the mission of the SFRY armed forces also includes maintaining the territorial integrity of the SFRY -- of the SFRY, excuse me, as well as the social order. So in case there are threats against the territorial integrity or social order from within, which then, according to the Supreme Command, i.e., the Presidency, warrant the use of the armed forces, well, then the conditions would be fulfilled to use the armed forces to act against such a threat.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Your answer is fairly satisfactory, with a brief addition. In case there was an attempt to forcefully change the constitutional system, it has to be a forcefully applied change for the supreme commander to act. We had a movement in the 1980s, and in that movement I was one of the formal dissidents, but we did not try to change the system by force. We did this by peaceful means, and then armed force could not be deployed, because if the armed forces were to be deployed, it would have to be a forcible attempt at changing the constitutional order. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I would just like to make a small correction to the transcript on page 85, line 25. It should read "Article 240" instead of "Article 214" of the 1974 SFRY Constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, what did the system of All People's or Total National Defence comprised of? What were the components of that system?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, in addition to the SFRY armed forces consisting of the JNA and the TO, there were also -- there was also a structure known as "civil defence" which was organised by republic. There was also a monitoring service, as well as maybe other bodies which I have not explicitly mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You don't know that, Mr. Theunens. The system of All People's Defence encompassed all the social subjects and individuals who were of age, citizens of age, adults, so the system was all-embracing. All the state organs, all the factories, all the social enterprises, all the social organisations, as well as political organisations, and indeed all individuals were the subjects in the system of All People's Defence or Total National Defence; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I misunderstood the question, then. Just to bring us back to my report, I state on page -- English page 4 that the whole of the population was involved in the -- under the doctrine of All People's Defence in order to defend the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, do you know what political organisations existed in communist Yugoslavia before the introduction of the multiparty system?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have a vague recollection of a number of organisations that existed, but I have not discussed them in my report because I did not consider them relevant for the subject matter of my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That was fairly important and relevant, Mr. Theunens, you know, because the League of Communists existed, the Socialist Alliance of the Working People of Yugoslavia existed as an organisation of the National Front, the Socialist Youth Alliance, the Student Alliance, as well as the Veterans Alliance, and even a trade union's association which had certain features of a political organisation in addition to trade union rights. All of them were political organisations, and each of them had its place and role in the system of All People's Defence; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have not analysed or studied the role of these various organisations in my report, so I'm not able to provide more information as to what Mr. Seselj has stated here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You must have done that. You necessarily had to do that, because during the examination-in-chief, Judge Antonetti drew your attention to the provisions of the law governing All People's Defence, and those provisions speak of the role of the League of Communists therein, and even in the sphere of command over the armed forces; isn't that right? The League of Communists had a certain role to play there as a political organisation; right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have not come across documents -- I mean, while studying the documents I have included in the report, I have not come across documents that indicate that the League of Communists intervened in operational matters or in command-and-control matters that are relevant in the context of my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The law states quite clearly what the role of the League of Communists is in military units. Do you happen to know that every JNA unit and every unit of the Territorial Defence had its own organisation, its own League of Communists organisation; do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, as we discussed in the examination, I am familiar with the existence of organs for morale and political guidance in the staffs and the commands of JNA and TO units, and the role of these organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now we have a legal system in which the role of the political organisations is defined within the sphere of the country's defence. The system is now changed. From a one-party system, it became a multiparty system. But all the legal provisions on the work of political organisations in the sphere of the country's defence remain the same. Why does the Serbian Radical Party, when it was formed, and it was registered officially in February 1991, why would it not have -- why would it not be one of the subjects in the country's defence with its inception? The League of Communists no longer exists. We have a multiparty system. There's nothing more logical -- well, you had one party before, and now you have many parties, but the role in each subject in the country's defence remains the same. Nobody changed that, or do you have proof to the contrary?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, but I just want to reiterate that the documents -- I mean, the regulations, the manuals, as well as the operational documents, orders and reports, I discussed in the report and I reviewed while preparing the report, do not mention anything about the role for political parties in the issues that are relevant in the context of my report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Expert witness, as I listen to the questions and answers, I was wondering whether, in terms of your method and approach, when you prepared your expert report, did you not see these issues from the standpoint of a European, in other words, somebody who was standing behind the famous curtain, and that you basically applied your world view to concepts which were different; in other words, you applied your German, Belgian, or whatever concept without factoring in this political information, in other words, that this part of the world was different and had its own internal workings, the role played by the League of Communists that disappeared but which was replaced by others like the Serbian Radical Party, and that at that time the doctrine or the concept of All People's Defence should be seen through the prism which prevailed before Yugoslavia's disintegration. Did you not ask yourself this question when doing your work, because the Belgian political parties, I assume, faced with a conflict, would have certainly played a part by having a bill adopted, but would have undoubtedly not played the same role as in the former Yugoslavia, where the political parties were playing a role. I even put the question to you, "Was there a political commissioner," and you said, yes, in so many words, because you said in some of the units there was somebody in charge of morale and other affairs, and what might be missing in your report is the fact that the workings of the system under Tito was not assessed as it should be.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do not think that I have applied a, call it, only or limited Western view to the problem I had to deal with, when considering especially part 1 of the report it is very obvious that the communist doctrine, at least the interpretation Tito had given to communist doctrine placed an essential role in the defence and the armed forces and how the armed forces function, their role and so on, even though, and I want to make a correction to what I think may have said during the first day of the examination, Yugoslavia or Serbia was never a member of the Warsaw Pact. Now, it is true that at the end of the 1980s, we see other political parties set up, there are multiparty elections in the course of 1990, but having reviewed an extensive number of military documents, I haven't come across any document that suggests that these other political parties are allowed to play a role in the armed forces or whether any of these political parties takes over the role, and morale and doctrine -- the ideological role that the League of Communists had. On the contrary, documents from security organs and other organs of the Security Administration, they keep a close eye on the various political parties that are emerging, both -- I mean, not only in Serbia but also in the other republics, and they are very suspicious of these other political parties, in particular when they try to infiltrate the armed forces. Now, coming now to the essential issue in this report, i.e., the role of volunteers, the legislation, as it existed in communist times, did not mention a role for political parties. The decrees and orders that are adopted between August 1991 and December 1991 do not make any mention of political parties, either in the recruitment or the training and so on of volunteers, so if these political parties had been allowed to play a role whatsoever, well, it would have been formalised somewhere. If these -- the non-communist political parties would have been allowed to participate in the elaboration or the implementation of the defence doctrine, it would have been put on paper somewhere. There would have been a trace. Well, there are no such traces. On the contrary, the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, now, if you adopt a Marxist view, if you look at the issue of All People's Defence in that light, everybody takes part in this, the trade unions, the associations, political parties, and so on and so forth. The best proof of this is you quoted Article 240 of the 1974 Constitution, and in the last paragraph it is mentioned that: "Any citizen who takes part in resistance against the aggressor is a member of the armed forces," which means that any citizen, including volunteers who are citizens, are automatically members of the armed forces. This is written in the Constitution. Therefore, the political parties can also adopt this notion of All People's Defence, but it seems that you do not draw the same conclusions in your report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, with political parties, if we mean the different political parties that emerged once the multiparty system was implemented, I can only reiterate that these parties, as such, while implementing their party programmes or party ideologies, did not play a role in the defence, at least de jure were not foreseen to play a role in the defence. It is obvious that in the situation prior to the existence of a multiparty system, whereby all the organisations that existed in the SFRY, labour organisations, syndicates, political movements, they all shared the same ideology, they all shared Tito's interpretation of the communist ideology or call it socialist ideology. That is not the case in the multiparty system, and that is exactly the issue I think that is of importance. You cannot have -- and that's not a Western view. That's, I think, a view that applies to any armed force. You cannot have a defence system where each party has its own component in the defence system, the blue party has something, the black party has something, the yellow party has something, because it would be a violation of the principle of unity in command and control. We have discussed earlier the analogy between All People's Defence and guerrilla warfare, or at least the doctrine or the concept -- concept as it was defined by Mao. As I said earlier, for Mao the ideology is the key component, but there's only one ideology. It's the communist, or call it socialist, ideology. So whatever party, as long as they share that ideology, or whatever organisation, as long as they share that ideology, they could play a role in the defence. However, when we come with other ideologies, for example, national ideologies, which go straight against -- against the key idea of the SFRY armed forces, i.e., brotherhood and unity, there is no role -- there cannot be a role for these parties in the defence of the country. And that's not just my interpretation. That's based on the documents I reviewed. Otherwise, looking at it from the opposite side, the SFRY authorities and SSNO would have had all interests in getting as many volunteers as possible if the political parties were allowed to play a role in the defence of the country, but Kadijevic and others had a very -- had a negative view. Okay, they legalise the volunteers because they have no other means. There is no response to mobilisation, or a very poor response, so they have to use these people, but not because they want the political parties to play a role in defence, but just because there's no other manpower available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have provided a rather lengthy answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a little bit lost. I might be mistaken, but I feel that all of this is not very relevant, has nothing much to do with our indictment and nothing much to do with the expert report. This was not designed to assess whether the participation of the volunteers was legitimate or not, whether the volunteers were to be part of All People's Defence or not, according to Yugoslav law. So the question, I believe, is a totally different question we would like to address. In the last part here, I must say that I'm a little bit at a loss.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honours, that it goes beyond the initial scope of my report, but I understand that there is a concern with the honourable Judges that actually there was nothing wrong with the fact that political parties mobilised or organised their own volunteers, as this was in any way foreseen by All People's Defence doctrine, which, as was pointed out in the Constitution and among other things, stated all citizens who participate, armed or not, in an aggression will be considered members of the armed forces. But what I tried to highlight in my reply is that all these laws and the doctrine existed or was established and was applied during the time that there was only one ideology, the communist or Tito's interpretation of communism or call it socialist ideology. And there were indeed many organisations -- there was the organisation of collective labour, students and so on and so forth, but they all shared one doctrine. It was not a multiparty system. The problem arises when multi or different political parties with different ideologies and sometimes ideologies that are opposite to the communist ideology feel that they have to play a role in the defence of the country, because they see, for example, that, well, we have here -- we can use nationalistic motives or ideology and try to use that ideology in the context of the armed forces, i.e., to influence the use of the armed forces. That is, in my understanding, not in line with or not coherent with the doctrine of All People's Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, who drew your attention to the fact that during the examination-in-chief, you made an error when you said that Yugoslavia left the Warsaw Pact in the 1950s?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honours, I think the session stopped in the -- around 1315, and when I cycled home, I realised that I had made an error, and I thought that -- I knew that Yugoslavia left or was removed from the Cominform [Realtime transcript read in error "common form"] at the time of Stalin because of a conflict between Tito and Stalin, and I wanted to be sure about the issue of the Warsaw Pact. And then I realised that actually Yugoslavia had never been a member of the Warsaw Pact, and that's how it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, who was with you on the bicycle and helped you realise that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether I have to answer that question, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, you consulted someone about the contents of your testimony, and whoever it was drew your attention to the error; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
