utterances.text: [Interpretation] Were you the person who checked out or were you helped, assisted, by someone? Of course, not by your bicycle, who cannot speak.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did it by myself, Your Honours. And to be really open, I looked at old course books I had from the military academy, I checked in that because it was something I wanted to be certain about. And in the history course in military academy, we, for example, we studied the Warsaw Pact and the establishment of the various Blocs in Europe and so on and so on, and this is how I finally then discovered that something I had stated was not entirely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, you've just stated that Yugoslavia left the Comintern. When did Yugoslavia leave the Comintern? The Communist International, that is.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought I mentioned the Cominform but, anyway, I think this happened at the end of the 1950s. I don't have a precise date, but I know it had to do with a conflict between Tito and Stalin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, how could Yugoslavia have left the Comintern in the 1950s when, by a decision of its competent organs, in 1943 the Comintern was dissolved? So Yugoslavia remained in it for ten years after its dissolution? How is that possible?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, there may be an issue in the transcript, but I used the term "Cominform" initially. "Cominform," not "common form." "Common forum."

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What is the Cominform, Mr. Theunens?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no exact recollection, Your Honours, of the nature of that organisation. I know that it included countries from Central and Eastern Europe and that the Soviet -- or the former Soviet Union had a leading role in it, but I cannot provide any additional information.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was the Cominform a kind of military alliance, Mr. Theunens?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What does it have to do with the Warsaw Pact, then?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an issue of the dates, Your Honour, and the relations between the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and various call it supranational or international organisations of communist countries, which there was Cominform, there was Warsaw Pact, and I had confused the two of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are you trying to say that the Cominform was a supranational organisation of communist countries; right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. What I'm trying to say is that it was an organisation of countries with a regime that could be qualified as communist or socialist, as they call it themselves, which were located primarily in Central and Eastern Europe, and that the former Soviet Union, led by Stalin, played a leading role in it. I'm sure that an expert in Cominform will be able to tell you much more about it, but this is what I can say about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, was the Cominform, C-O-M-I-N-F-O-R-M, an international organisation?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my recollection, Your Honours, it included various countries in Central and Eastern Europe which were led by communist or, as they call themselves, socialist regimes. And as it includes different countries, it could be called international.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, what, in your view, is the definition of an international organisation? What does an international organisation encompass?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe there's confusion, Your Honours, with "supranational" and "international," but, anyway, "international" for me means that it includes countries or members of different countries. There can be an international football competition.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Let's simplify matters. You're almost right. International organisations are organisations of state, would you agree, such as the United Nations, such as the European Community was before the Union was formed, such as the NATO Pact, such as ACN, such as the Arab League, such as the Organisation of African Unity; those are all organisations of states, are they not?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And the Cominform is an information bureau of communist and workers' parties. It has nothing to do with states. It's an information bureau of communist and workers' parties to which the French and Italian communists also belonged, although they were not the ruling parties in their countries; isn't that right? The problem is, Mr. Theunens, that you know nothing. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether I have to answer the question, Your Honours, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What you call "common forum" in English, does it refer to the Communist International?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was referring to the -- I can spell it, the C-O-M-I-N-F-O-R-M. It's not "forum" but it's "form," which in my understanding was an organisation where countries from Central and Eastern Europe cooperated together with the Soviet Union. There may be other members. As I stated, I'm not a specialist in the COMINFORM. But what I remember is that at one point in time Tito decides to leave the League of Communists, to leave the COMINFORM following a conflict with Stalin which had been ongoing already for a long time. And the only reason I mentioned the COMINFORM was that I confused the two organisations when I said that it was that Yugoslavia left the Warsaw Pact in the end of the 1950s, because it actually left the COMINFORM, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It's still not clear to you, Mr. Theunens, that the COMINFORM is an international organisation of communist and workers' parties, because Italy and France were never communist states, but their communist parties were members of the Cominform; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, that's right, and I should actually clarify that it's the Yugoslav League of Communists that left the Cominform, which seems to be difficult to spell, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But you did not know that when you were supposed to explain it, because you kept on insisting that the Cominform is an organisation or an association of countries, of states. When was Tito's Yugoslavia a member of a military alliance, and of what alliance if it was, do you know?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my recollection, Tito's Yugoslavia was never a member of a military alliance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, I would immediately invalidate your diploma which you got from the Belgian Military document, because from 1953 to 1956, Tito's Yugoslavia was a member of the Balkan League with Greece and Turkey, and it was treated as an extension of the NATO pact, and only when Greece and Turkey joined the NATO pact directly did the Balkan League die out. I think you are no officer, but maybe Belgium can tolerate this because it has a long military tradition.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Seselj repeat his question, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Theunens, Mr. Seselj is saying that between 1956 and 1966 --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1953 and 1956.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Between 1953 and 1956, in other words, for three years, apparently, Yugoslavia was a member of the Balkan Alliance, together with Greece and Turkey, and it was only when Greece entered NATO that Yugoslavia left this alliance. Did you know this or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Apparently not now, Your Honours. Otherwise, I would not -- I wouldn't have made such an oversight. But I may have known in the past, but I didn't remember at this stage.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My next question was: In 1946 [as interpreted], for how long did Belgium resist Hitler's soldatesque?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1940, not 1946. There's a mistake in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1940, I guess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Relevance, I suppose. Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Yes. It's irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I questioning the credibility, Mr. President. I'm challenging the witness's credibility. I have the right to challenge the expert's credibility in this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Theunens, the accused is testing your knowledge by asking you questions related to history. How long did Belgium resist in 1940?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no exact recollection. It was not a matter of a month.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was it hours and minutes, Mr. Theunens?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've answered the question, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He's answered.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He doesn't know, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He's not a historian, anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But at the military academy, he must have learned about the heroic traditions of the Belgian Army, Madam Judge. In Serbian military academies we are constantly learning about the heroic traditions of the Serbian Army. I suppose Belgium must have a heroic tradition also, but, very well, I'll move on. I couldn't resist putting this question to him, because I have to show you what an absolute ignoramus this expert witness is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, are you aware that in communist Yugoslavia, there were special volunteer units?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's an objection, because you said that the expert didn't know anything. Mr. Marcussen, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: That is my objection. The accused might very well have this kind of opinion about the witness, but it's not proper language before the Court.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can speak about it either in prison or in the courtroom. I have no further place to say this. But I do have to say that this alleged expert is an ignoramus, but I'll put another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, do you know that in communist Yugoslavia, there were special volunteer units?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you may well say that the expert is not a true expert, but there's no need to tell him that he's ignorant. The two things are quite different.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me remind you, Mr. President, of a historical precedent of the trial of Oscar Wilde. Whatever it was possible to say in cross-examination then, I can say here now. But I am much less severe than those who participated in that trial. I can't recognise, myself, when I see how good-natured I am towards the false witnesses and experts of the OTP. I have two more questions before we conclude for today, because that's one stage of my cross-examination which will then be rounded off.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, are you aware that in communist Yugoslavia, there was special volunteer detachments within the system of All People's Defence?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm aware of the definition I took for volunteer units from the 1981 military lexicon, which is discussed on English page 72 of part 1 of my report, where, indeed, mention is made of volunteer units tracing back to history not only in Yugoslavia but also outside of Yugoslavia, and making mention of the existence of volunteer units in Yugoslavia, even though the focus seems to be on the Second World War. I have not come across information indicating the existence of volunteer units under the doctrine of All People's Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, if I say to you that as a pupil in the third form of secondary school, I became a member of a volunteer unit of the Territorial Defence of the City of Sarajevo and that I participated in an inspection of the units of the Territorial Defence conducted by General Franjo Heljevic [phoen] and the commander of the city staff, Colonel Stefan Valter reported to him, and I stood in the front row and held a semi-automatic rifle on my shoulder, would you believe me? And I was a pupil in the third form of secondary school, of grammar school. Do you believe me, that that's how it was?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, if -- or, Your Honours, if Mr. Seselj says so, then I don't know -- I don't see a reason why I should not believe him. But what I said, when I answered that I have not come across --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, the question is not an entirely innocent question as regards the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party, because if before the 1990, 1991, 1993 events, if before that there was a volunteer system established in Yugoslavia, and he gave you the example of the fact that when he was still a schoolboy, he was part and parcel of a military unit, so it's quite possible that this was natural in the former Yugoslavia, this existence of volunteer units who participated together with the army to the implementation of this all defence concept, but then why didn't you study this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't think it's a matter of me not studying something. It's more a matter of me looking at documents and drawing conclusions from these documents. As we discussed during my testimony, the concept of volunteers is defined in the law. The legal references also give a minimal age for volunteers. I mean, these legal references, I have included in my report, and if I'm not wrong, the minimum age was 18 years old. So if school children organised in one way or the other and even have to carry an automatic weapon, based on my understanding of the system, that is not the same as the legally-defined volunteers as they are -- as they are described in, for example, the 1982 All People's Defence Law or the later decrees, where a minimum age a maximum age, as well as other conditions are explained. I have not come across information indicating in legislation or doctrine indicating that school children could join volunteer units and what these volunteer units then would do in case of an armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, put your last question, because it's already 1.15. We have to close. I think you had a last question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may put a sub-question in connection with this one, and then I'll put my next question. I'd like to draw Mr. Theunens' attention to the following: In 1972, I was almost 18. I became a member of a unit two or three months before my 18th birthday. We had special uniforms. Berets were introduced for the first time for volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But my last question for today is the following: If I were to say to you that as a student of the Faculty of Law, I was a member of volunteer students teaching the detachment, which comprised about 100 members, and that I personally, according to the guidelines and the way the Territorial Defence was organised, as a member of the faculty committee of the league of students, I formed this detachment for which the faculty bought uniforms from the Territorial Defence staff, would you believe me if I gave you that information?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no reason not to believe the information. I just want to reiterate that in the context of the preparation of my report, the documents I have reviewed, especially those dealing with the components of the SFRY armed forces, JNA and TO, whereby it is also stated that any armed structure that is not incorporated in the JNA shall be part of the TO, there is no specific mention of student units or other volunteer units. But in the concept or in the doctrine of All People's Defence, I have no reason to not to believe what Mr. Seselj is saying.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just explain the essence of this question, Mr. President. I was the president of the League of Students of the Faculty of Law. The Faculty Committee of the Faculty of Law, carrying out its role as a political organisation within the system of All People's Defence, formed students teaching volunteer detachment. It was called "Mosa Pijade" after a well-known communist revolutionary from between the two world wars. It was a political organisation of students which formed this teaching detachment, and that was within the system of territorial defence. I assume that you are surprised by this fact which I am telling you now. Isn't that right, Mr. Theunens? You had no idea about this?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, as we discussed when talking about All People's Defence, I'm not surprised by this, because I think one important aspect is that here it's explicitly authorised by the authorities. When we go back to the Article 118 of the 1990 Law on Defence of the Republic of Serbia, it is clearly stated that only the state authorities are allowed to plan, organise, equip, train armed forces. So if the authorities, in the context of the implementation of the concept of All People's Defence, believe that it is necessary to organise students into one form of defence, is it civil defence, is it -- are these volunteers to be members of the TO or whatever, that's all fine, but it's important to notice that it is -- it is in line or it is the result of the decision of the authorities and it is coherent with the ideology of All People's Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We continue tomorrow, starting at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
